subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, could the Secretary of State for External Affairs tell the house whether Canada has received a request from the secretary general of the United Nations to provide additional troops for the UN Cyprus force, and what has been the reaction thereto? Furthermore, is he now in a position to advise on any developments that took place at the meeting of the nine participating countries with the secretary general? Would he at the same time give his observations to the house as to what he believes will be the effect on the already delicate negotiations for a peaceful settlement in Cyprus of the appointment of the guerrilla leader, General Grivas, as commander of the Cypriot national guard, especially in view of the fact that the United Nations commander has stated that General Grivas regards the United Nations peace force as "a bloody nuisance"?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no comments to make at this time on the reported observation of General Grivas. With regard to the first part of my right hon. friend's question, there has been no formal request made to Canada for the supply of additional troops, although I believe General Thimayya has indicated he would like to see the United Nations forces brought up to the strength contemplated by the permissible limits under the security council resolution. At present Canada has 1,125 military personnel in Cyprus. Ours is the largest contingent in the United Nations force except for that supplied by Britain which is only slightly larger.
A meeting of the contributors took place yesterday at the United Nations. The Canadian ambassador expressed the view of the Canadian government that all possible measures should be taken to enhance the authority of the force so it would be in a more favourable position to carry out its assigned task. There will be further consultations, and I am confident that the position taken by the Canadian government is being urgently considered by the commander of the force.
In addition, Mr. Galo Plaza, a former president of Ecuador and a man of considerable experience in and outside the United Nations, is returning to Cyprus to carry on negotiations as the representative of the secretary general in discussions with the force commander as well as with the Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot authorities. Admittedly the United Nations force, as the secretary general has publicly stated, is working within fairly circumscribed limits. Failing agreement in the security council and in addition the formal agreement of the Cypriot authorities, an extension of the powers of the force need not necessarily be expected. What we are doing is to maintain our representations to the United Nations authorities to ensure that all possible measures are pursued to enable the force to operate effectively within its present mandate.
From the report we received from our ambassador this morning I can say that the secretary general is determined to see that the principle of freedom of movement, as embodied in the exchange of notes between himself and the government of Cyprus, is established. To this end Mr. Galo Plaza as well as General Thimayya will be engaged in consultation with appropriate authorities.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext:
May I ask a supplementary question. In view of the use of the words, which I took down, that the augmentation of the powers of the force ''need not necessarily be expected", may we take it that is a diplomatic way of saying there is going to be no increase in those powers? This expression is strangely reminiscent of the phrase "conscription if necessary, but not necessarily conscription." Do the words so carefully enunciated by the minister indicate that the force will continue to operate under
6812	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry powers that have proven insufficient for that force to properly discharge its responsibilities?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext: I would agree as to "insufficient", but it could not be argued that as a result of this insufficiency the United Nations is not playing a very important role in these very difficult circumstances. No; my hon. friend should not read anything into my language that was carefully conceived before being uttered. It simply means that we cannot, in this house, take unto ourselves powers which belong to the security council and which in turn can only be given effect to following agreement with the government of Cyprus. These are limitations that exist, and we will not further our objectives in this situation by failing to recognize them. Within those limitations I think my right hon. friend has now been informed of our intentions.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question in the light of reports that the secretary general of the United Nations is requesting the participating countries to supply additional troops for the peace keeping force in Cyprus. In the event that Canada is asked to do so, will this matter be referred to parliament before the request is complied with? Second, would the Canadian government make the supplying of additional Canadian troops contingent upon some amendment of the agreement of status to include provision for disarming guerrillas?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext:
I would not agree to such a condition, myself. This might be a desirable condition to impose in normal circumstances; but if it is not attainable, and if we were faced with the alternative of either having this condition accepted or of making no contribution to a situation that requires an international force, I would not be prepared to accept it even though this would be the easiest position to take.
With regard to the position of parliament concerning an increase in the numbers of the Canadian force, the resolution of this house authorizes the government to provide up to 1,200 men. If there were any disposition to go beyond that figure then of course we would have to come back to this house. I have pointed out that the Canadian contribution now is greater than that of any other of the participating countries except Britain. The secretary general and General Thimayya are undoubtedly giving consideration to the possibility of additional contributions of forces from others of the participating countries. I
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext: As a further supplementary question, in view of the fact that the obstacle does not seem to lie with the security council of the United Nations but rather with the government of Cyprus, would the minister not agree that if additional forces are to be requested to protect the people of Cyprus, the very least Canada has a right to expect is the co-operation of the government of Cyprus in amending the agreement of status so as to make that force effective?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext: Of course Canada has the right to expect, and not only Canada but the whole world, that there will be this measure of co-operation; but this is something that depends on the government of Cyprus and possibly as well on other governments. The force could not I think be augmented beyond the present 7,000 figure without the approval of the security council. There may be some hesitation in confronting the security council because of attitudes that could conceivably be taken by other countries. I am not saying that this situation would arise, but this may be in the mind of the secretary general.

Courts have been established at Toronto, Montreal, Hamilton, London, Vancouver, Edmonton, Winnipeg, Moncton, Windsor and Ottawa.
These courts along with the regularly constituted courts provide facilities for persons wishing to apply for Canadian citizenship. There are in addition 56 persons who have been appointed courts for the purpose of the Canadian Citizenship Act in areas in Canada remote from regularly constituted courts.
6818	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Four similar appointments have been made overseas to assist servicemen who wish to become Canadian citizens.
Persons applying for citizenship through courts must first satisfy the court that the several statutory requirements set forth in the act have been met before the application may be processed by the branch headquarters in Ottawa.
I am pleased to inform the hon. members who have expressed an interest in the qualifications which must be met by an applicant for Canadian citizenship, that a review has been made of the standard required of applicants and that certain amendments to the citizenship act are to be introduced into parliament shortly that will facilitate the acquisition of citizenship. This is in keeping with the policy of the Liberal party. At the same time, it will be recommended that provisions which now discriminate between naturalized and natural-born Canadians be removed from the act. The regulations to the Canadian Citizenship Act have been amended to include a provision to schedule B that will permit veterans of the armed forces of Canada who were on active service during time of war and who have not previously been naturalized, to be exempt from the payment of the fee of $10 required under item 8 of the same schedule. I am also endeavouring to establish uniform criteria for the use of courts in the administration of citizenship across Canada.
In 1963, 69,468 persons became Canadian citizens. This is fourth highest number for any one year; the highest was in 1957 when 95,462 certificates were granted. From January 1, 1947, to December 31, 1963, a total of 723,847 persons have been granted citizenship in Canada. In addition, approximately
460,000	certificates were issued to persons who wished to have proof of their status as Canadians.
The number of applications fluctuates from year to year, but it is known that about 40 per cent of the immigrants who entered Canada during the past ten years who were eligible for Canadian citizenship have became Canadians.
It has been found that fitting and appropriate ceremonies for the presentation of certificates of citizenship can focus a great deal of attention on the benefits to new Canadians of the acquisition of Canadian citizenship. I am therefore encouraging more participation by voluntary organizations in citizenship ceremonies. For the same reason, an item has been included in the estimates to provide for


the expansion of the jurisdiction of some of the present courts and for the opening of a new court of Canadian citizenship in Calgary, Alberta. At the same time I shall give continuing study to the opening of courts in other areas not yet serviced by a court of Canadian citizenship.
The Canadian citizenship branch could be described as the extension arm of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. It will be appreciated that much of the work of my department is concerned with the fulfilment of the hopes and aspirations of special categories of persons. A civil service, no matter what their number or dedication, cannot replace the personal interest that needs to be shown by the average citizen if the goals I seek are to be attained. In carrying out its responsibilities, the citizenship branch encourages and assists individuals, groups and agencies that are interested in immigrants, Indians and general citizenship to play a more effective role.
The data from a survey of language classes for immigrants, which I am reviewing at present, will be used in discussions with various agencies offering English or French language instruction, with a view to improving the courses offered and rendering them as attractive as possible to immigrants. I have directed the officials to intensify their efforts in order that more citizenship courses are offered in conjunction with language classes. Such courses will enable applicants for Canadian citizenship to become more familiar with Canadian institutions and traditions, in preparation for the court examination which non-British subjects must take when applying for Canadian citizenship.
Hon. members are aware of the public interest evidenced in recent years, most dynamically, in the organization of Indian friendship councils and centres in a large number of communities across Canada and in the emergence of two national organizations, the national Indian council and the Indian-Eskimo association. The citizenship branch will increase its activities in this field in co-operation with these organizations, which add security that Indians need to feel when off their reserves and which make it easier for them to live in communities that offer the type of work they would like to have.
In respect of general citizenship, the branch will be asked to play an active role in encouraging and helping Canadians to participate fully in centennial celebrations. It is our hope that 1967 will be an occasion

for all Canadians to become more aware of the historical development of our country and the cultural heritage that has accumulated during the past 100 years.
May I take this opportunity to offer some observations on the subject of immigration as it affects Canada. This is the first opportunity I have had to acquaint the committee in any extensive manner with my views on this subject which is one of paramount importance to all of us.
Because of limitations of time I shall not deal at length with the contribution which the new Canadians have made to the general Canadian welfare. It is a study well worthwhile in itself. I could not make this statement, however, without saying that the Canadian economy and our culture simply could not have advanced either quantitatively or qualitatively to their present state without the very substantial contribution of these thousands of immigrants. We owe thanks to those who have come to us in the period under discussion.
We come now to the question of where we stand at this moment in the matter of Canada's domestic concern with immigration and the need for policy in this field to meet the needs of 1964 and the years beyond.
Mr. Chairman, before proceeding with this question I should like to explain what I mean by the term "skilled" which I shall be using in this statement from time to time. In my view this is a fairly broad term which includes a variety of persons. It includes those with a reasonably good level of education sufficient to permit a range of mobility and adaptability required in most occupations today. These persons should also have qualifications in their particular fields. In terms of the trades which are common in Canada, these qualifications would normally mean the possession of journeymen's papers or certificates of competency. The term "skilled" also includes those with more advanced technical or professional training, as well as those with successful experience as managers or proprietors of commercial, industrial and agricultural activities.
While in years past there was a need for the immigration of unskilled and semi-skilled workers in large numbers, this is no longer the case. The Canada of 1964 is not the Canada of 1913, 1946 or even 1954. Machines now aid manpower in many areas of activity. In some fields, such as agriculture, fewer workers actually produce far more than ever before. Technological advancements are caus-
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration ing sweeping alterations in the pattern of employment.
This committee does not need to be told that the greatest handicap of the majority of our unfortunate unemployed is a lack of education or skill. Our government has committed and spent substantial funds for the training and re-training of those who lack the necessary skills for today's employment market. This year's budget, in providing for family allowances for children in school beyond 16 years of age, emphasized certain aspects of our concern today about those who leave formal training inadequately prepared.
At the same time, there is a very substantial demand and need for skilled individuals in many undertakings across Canada. The presence of such workers provides a stimulus to the enterprise and the economy of this country. Unfortunately, these persons are not always available from within Canada or, if here, are not sufficiently mobile to fill particular opportunities. Then too, in this country-as in any country-there is abundant scope for managerial talent, as well as for those with the experience, ability and funds to establish their own enterprises.
The competition we must meet in today's world is a competition of brains, skill, ability and initiative. Despite our best efforts and whatever our virtues at this moment, we cannot claim a surplus of any of these features. We must overlook no opportunity to encourage additional people who can assist us, to come to this country.
To this end, and as a first principle of this government's immigration policy, we shall endeavour-through adequate promotion and recruitment-to bring to Canada the well-skilled on a substantial scale. This is to be a positive program. It will help to fill the gaps in our industry, commerce, and other areas of economic activity here. Increased activity across the board will aid in absorbing the unskilled amongst us.
At the same time, the infusion of skilled people will assist in developing further the better balanced and even more dynamic economic structure we will need to absorb the greatly increased entries to the labour force from Canadian sources which will soon take place, due to our own rapidly expanding population, a feature that will be even more important in the next six to eight years.
It is impossible to make any valid predictions of the exact numbers of immigrants during a period ahead of, say, a year. This
6820	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration is increasingly the case in present circumstances. On the one hand, our economic capacity to absorb skilled, educated and otherwise well-qualified immigrants is virtually unlimited. On the other hand, this type of person is in demand in many countries these days. We must obtain these immigrants in competition with other countries and there is no great surplus of qualified people anywhere in the world.
To help establish a more positive immigration program our government has taken the following steps:
(a)	We have provided for an interdepartmental committee composed of senior officials well versed in economic, labour and social problems to assess our needs, and our absorptive capacity, for migrants in Canada's economy. This committee, which will serve in an advisory capacity, should help the government in its objective of developing fairly long term programs not subject to the turning on and off of the immigration tap which has had such objectionable results in the past.
(b)	We are embarking on a considerably increased promotional campaign abroad, particularly in Europe where the greatest number of likely immigration applicants are to be found. Additional funds for this purpose are contained in the estimates before you.
(c)	The government recently approved a new establishment structure for immigration personnel abroad. This is a first step in our plans to ensure better classifications for our personnel in order to implement a really productive and positive immigration program.
(d)	The existing organization, served as it is by many hard working and capable people, is not such as to get the maximum results from our immigration efforts. The organization must be made fully responsive to today's immigration requirements. It is very short of staff, particularly in its overseas service. If the effort to secure adequate numbers of immigrants with the skills Canada needs is to succeed, we require more and better trained personnel and we must see that they are employed to maximum advantage in posts for which they are best qualified. We must hold open the opportunity to pursue a career for these employees, a career satisfying to the person concerned and as fully rewarding as any comparable posts in the public service. A complete re-organization in immigration, both at home and abroad, is overdue. It is now in the course of development.
(e)	Not only are changes in organization required with appropriate staffing, but so also are changes badly needed in the picture


Canada presents overseas in so far as its immigration offices and facilities are concerned. These have been too often dull and unattractive. Every effort will be made, consistent with good and efficient management, to secure office locations and quarters that will do Canada justice, enable our staff to work effectively, and promote a favourable reaction among potential immigrants. Such steps will enable us to compete on more equal grounds with other countries which are also making strong efforts to secure the immigrants they need. Let me say that in our efforts to promote immigration abroad, this government will welcome the participation of the provincial governments wherever they feel they can be of help. In addition, it is the intention of the government to discuss immigration matters with certain foreign governments in the hope we can achieve a better understanding of our operations and ambitions in the immigration field.
We come now to the second principle of this government's immigration policy. It has to do with the social-and in some respects-the humanitarian aspects of immigration. I refer to our intention to do what we can to assist in the reunion of families-with particular regard to the immediate family, that is, the head of the family and his dependents-and to assist refugees.
In the past the department has received criticism from some quarters where sponsored immigration is concerned, on two main points. First, the length of waiting period in some countries has been unduly long before relatives can be examined for immigration purposes. Second, there has appeared to be inconsistency on the part of immigration offices within Canada, in assessing the adequacy or otherwise of the reception arrangement which can be provided by the sponsor here.
With regard to the first point, the waiting period for examination in Hong Kong for example has been reduced from nine months to three. We hope to effect even further improvement in this respect not only with regard to that area, but in connection with the selection of immigrants everywhere. This, of course, is not the end but the beginning.
I am very conscious of the desirability and even the necessity of re-establishing families, of bringing together again a man, his wife and their dependent children, without avoidable delay. All the procedures and practices within the department are under my systematic and critical review. The procedures governing our operations in this particular area are being dealt with on a priority basis.

Furthermore, the moves being made for more qualified staff and better facilities which I have already mentioned, are under way with this problem very much in mind. Within a reasonable period I hope to be able to report to this committee that waiting periods for examination of immigrants have been reduced to an absolute minimum.
I should like at this time to say a few words on my visit earlier this year to Hong Kong. Several important conclusions and decisions have resulted from that trip which will be of interest to hon. members. I also visited Japan where I had the pleasure of very informative and fruitful discussions with officials of the Japanese government.
This was the first of a number of inspection visits which I hope to make, as minister, to learn first hand the facts on which to base a development of new immigration policies and programs. Early in September I expect to leave for an inspection trip of immigration offices in Europe and while there, I plan to consult with government officials in the various countries. I chose Hong Kong for my first visit because I was deeply concerned about the complex problems involved in Chinese immigration and complaints I had received that our Hong Kong operation was inefficient and discriminatory.
I found Hong Kong prosperous and thriving. It is a model of efficient administration for which the British authorities deserve great praise. The flow of illegal immigrants from mainland China has declined to a trickle, and the population situation is now more stable. You will note that I do not use the term "refugees" in relation to those persons leaving mainland China. The British maintain, and I agree, that these people are not political refugees at all, but are simply seeking a better economic life. This is proven by the fact that once they are accepted as Hong Kong residents they flock back to China to visit by the hundreds of thousands, apparently without fear of persecution.
I also learned in Hong Kong that the British authorities do not regard mass emigration as a solution to their population problems. They feel that if it becomes known that Hong Kong is an easy stepping stone to Canada or the United States the colony would receive hundreds more migrants from the mainland for every immigrant who goes to North America.
Therefore, while Canada can offer a better future to some individuals from Hong Kong,
any large scale program of resettlement here

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration would do more harm than good as far as Hong Kong is concerned. Therefore, my first conclusion was that we must look at immigration from Hong Kong in ordinary immigration terms rather than as a special refugee problem.
Even though Chinese from Hong Kong are not to be given any special refugee status, I must emphasize that the ordinary immigrant admissible classes, as they affect Chinese, are broad: they permit the admission of the immediate families, parents, grandparents and fiancees of Canadian residents, as well as unsponsored immigrants who have sufficient education or skills to become established in Canada.
In addition there is another less well-known admissible class, of which even many of the Chinese seem unaware. This permits Canadian citizens to sponsor the admission of such non-dependent relatives as adults or married sons or daughters, along with the spouse and children of such sons and daughters. These non-dependents are sponsorable in the usual way subject to appropriate educational and occupational standards.
It can be seen, therefore, that the legal admissible classes do not create any impossible barrier to the reunion of Chinese families in Canada. However, the law does require that each immigrant, whether of Chinese origin or not, be examined to find out if he qualifies for admission, to ensure that he is not a criminal or subversive and, in the case of sponsored persons, to ensure that they have the relationship claimed to the sponsor in Canada.
The greatest problem we face in examining immigrants from mainland China is the difficulty in verifying their identities. Such immigrants arrive in Hong Kong with virtually no identifying documents. There are no official records available which can be used to verify the statements of the individual. This situation has given rise to extensive abuse in Chinese immigration with which present and past Canadian governments have attempted to cope.
There is evidence that many Chinese immigrants to Canada are in this country illegally. During my stay in Hong Kong I personally discussed the problem of illegal immigration with the immigration officials of other countries. All these countries experience the same problems that Canada does. They agree that there exists a well-organized and highly efficient illegal Chinese immigration system involving forged documents and photographs,
6822	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration schools that coach immigrants in false identities, persistent use of false statutory declarations, and other abuses.
Some Canadians are relatively unconcerned about illegal Chinese immigration. They feel that past discrimination has forced Chinese to use illegal means to get their dependents to Canada.
Our investigations have satisfied us that frequently relatives and friends, no doubt largely influenced by ties of blood and sympathy, have been parties to such illegal entries.
Often these admissions were arranged by syndicates or individuals who make a business of smuggling inadmissible persons into Canada from Hong Kong.
I am also satisfied that, contrary to popular belief, a large number of these illegal Chinese immigrants are not close relatives of Canadian residents. They were brought here solely for the profit of illegal immigration agents. This is a serious and disturbing situation. Not only does it tarnish the reputation of Chinese Canadians as good citizens, but it has added greatly to their problems when they seek to bring out their true relatives.
Speaking personally and for my department, I wish to emphasize that we have no desire to penalize Chinese Canadians seeking to bring their legitimate families to Canada.
During my visit to Hong Kong, and in subsequent discussions with departmental officials, every effort has been made to find ways to facilitate the admission of legal immigrants without destroying or weakening essential controls.
I found in Hong Kong that there are many changes which can be made in our system there that will facilitate the admission of close relatives to Canada. We have already reduced the waiting period for immigrants in Hong Kong from nine months to less than three, and I hope it can be reduced still further. The quickest way of improving the situation would be to provide more immigration staff in Hong Kong but for the time being extra staff cannot be accommodated in our Hong Kong office. We have already enlarged our staff as much as our office space will permit, and we are seeking larger office quarters. There is a severe shortage of office space in Hong Kong but we are trying to reserve space in a building now being erected. With larger and better quarters in Hong Kong and with certain other changes we should be able to deal with Chinese immigrants on a current basis without abnormal delays.


It is worthy of note, however, that, notwithstanding the shortage of staff and shortage of office space in Hong Kong, last year immigration of Chinese to Canada increased substantially. In 1963, some 1,571 Chinese were admitted as compared with a total of 876 in 1962. In the first five months of this year 879 were admitted as against 481 during the same period in 1963. In other words, the number of Chinese immigrants in 1963 increased almost 100 per cent over the figure for 1962 and has again increased 84 per cent in the first five months of this year as compared with the same period in 1963.
It is obvious, therefore, that as a direct result of the policies of this government and the changes in procedures which have been effected since this government took office hundreds of Chinese families have emigrated to Canada and hundreds more have been re-united in this country.
A serious problem for immigrants in Hong Kong is the necessity to visit various offices for medical tests and examinations. This is tedious, causes long waits and is expensive for the migrants.
I am discussing with my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh), the establishment of a completely integrated "one-stop" medical centre in our immigration office in Hong Kong. This would greatly benefit the immigrants.
There are in Hong Kong many well-qualified persons who have no relatives in Canada but who would make good immigrants. In the past, the department has been so preoccupied with servicing sponsored immigrants that little time was available for the unsponsored. This has been partially remedied and when we are in new quarters in Hong Kong, it should be possible to devote more of our resources to unsponsored immigrants without in any way interfering with the processing of the sponsored. Since sponsored immigrants are not usually skilled, it is desirable that this humanitarian flow be balanced by a movement of well-qualified unsponsored persons.
There are other changes which are being made in our office systems and routines, and our staffing and staff training policies, which should further improve our performance. These are matters of internal administration but I expect the results will soon speak for themselves.

Mr. Chairman, I am happy to say that my visit to Hong Kong satisfied me that our Canadian visa and medical officers, and our local Chinese staff are honest, extremely hard working public servants who have been doing a good job in the face of very difficult circumstances. I certainly do not want my comments on the needed improvements in the system to be considered as a reflection on their integrity or their devotion to duty. I have the greatest respect and regard for them all.
The foregoing has dealt with our administrative problems in connection with Chinese immigration. As a result of my trip I have also reached several general conclusions about the legal admissible classes and immigration policy as they apply to Chinese and I wish to speak of them at this time.
First, the admissible classes.
On the whole, the present admissible classes are adequate to permit a healthy Chinese immigration movement and the reunion of families. However, I am pleased to advise the house that the approval of the governor in council has just been given to one important addition to the admissible classes, and that is to make male fiances admissible on the same legal basis as female fiancees. This amendment will benefit particularly the Canadian Chinese community but will have the happy corollary of satisfying the justifiable ambitions of other ethnic groups.
I am not recommending at present that sponsorship privileges for Chinese be extended to cover brothers, sisters and more distant relatives. I regret this but unfortunately there are serious practical difficulties involved. An expansion of the admissible classes to cover these non-dependents would seriously interfere with the good service we propose to give to the immediate dependents. In addition it would multiply the problem of control and detection of impostors to an extent far beyond our present experience and would render ineffective our efforts to exercise essential controls. This decision is dictated solely by the facts of the situation and not by any desire to discriminate against Chinese.
Second, the Chinese status adjustment program.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
The Chinese have complained that this program is discriminatory. Actually the status adjustment system was intended to benefit the Chinese but its purpose has been misunderstood. Moreover, it has had limited success in spite of the fact that it has been in operation for four years, far longer than was anticipated. While we would not wish to discourage Chinese from voluntarily coming to our offices to set their personal immigration records straight we shall no longer exercise forbearance in respect of immigration violations merely because such voluntary statements are made. Everyone has had ample time to put his affairs in order and henceforth from September 1, 1964, R.C.M.P. and immigration officers are being instructed to apply the law to Chinese in exactly the same way as to other residents of Canada.
In concluding my remarks on Chinese immigration, I wish to say that, as Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, it is my aim to develop a positive immigration program to bring more well-qualified immigrants to this country and assist residents of Canada to reunite their dependent families here. Chinese immigration increased substantially last year and I firmly expect this increase to continue without loss of control over illegal immigration.
It is the sincere wish of this government, as I am sure it is of all Canadians of good will, to treat our Chinese compatriots as fairly as possible and make available to them the same facilities and opportunities provided to other citizens for the reunion of their families in this country and the prosperity of their community. If this desirable objective is to be attained it is essential that we have the wholehearted co-operation of the Chinese community, the vast majority of whose members are honest and reputable Canadians, in eliminating the abuses which have been of concern to all law-abiding citizens.
I should also say a word or two about my brief visit in Japan, during which I met the Japanese foreign minister and had informal talks with Japanese economic and emigration officials.
Emigration from Japan to Canada has been negligible in recent years, averaging less than 200 annually. Even with the change in immigration regulations in 1962, opening up immigration from all parts of the world, there was little interest shown by the Japanese, as indicated by the few applications received from that country.
There are several explanations for this. First, Japan's economy is booming and there
6824	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration are actually labour shortages in many skilled occupations. Japanese workers have ample opportunities at home. Moreover, Japan's emigration has, in the past, been organized in group settlements and the Japanese are accustomed to applying for migration in schemes organized by their own government rather than for individual migration. On the other hand, Canada's society is today so complex and highly developed that it is not possible for us to introduce large group settlements of one ethnic origin, and our entire immigration system is based on individual and family selection and settlement in Canada.
In our discussions we did much to clarify our respective viewpoints. Also, I endeavoured to convince the Japanese that any of their people who do qualify and are admitted to Canada will be assisted by our immigration service to locate jobs and homes and, in general, will be aided as fully as they would be in one of their own government-organized group settlements.
In view of the present economic conditions in Japan, it is not realistic to expect that any large scale immigration movement will result. But I am confident that steps have been taken which will result in a growing movement to Canada of qualified Japanese professional and technical workers and their families.
I should refer to another point in immigration procedures concerning apparent inconsistencies in assessing the abilities of sponsors to receive and care for their relatives until the latter have become established in Canada. Let me say first of all that this has rarely been a problem in recent years where the spouse and dependent children of a sponsor in Canada have been involved. The department takes a lenient view in such cases and the financial and domestic arrangements required have been reasonably easy to meet.
The sponsoring of relatives other than dependents is, however, a different matter, as I think all members will agree. The responsibilities assumed by the sponsor in Canada are serious ones. They include the willingness and ability to provide care and maintenance as need be until the immigrant and his family establish themselves in Canada. It was in assessing the abilities of various sponsors to meet these responsibilities that there may have been some variance of opinion on the part of different immigration officers.
To overcome this problem my officers, after intensive study, have developed more objective standards of assessing settlement ar-


rangements. These standards, which are essentially financial, were put into effect last February, upon my arrival in the department. Reports to date indicate that they are working out well, and in large measure have resolved the problem. Applicants who are unable to satisfy the criteria-which I believe to be reasonable-are informed of those deficiencies that must be overcome to have their applications approved. As I say, this system appears to be operating well; however, I shall keep it under review to ensure that it serves the purpose intended.
In the field of refugees, also, we intend to pursue those policies which have enabled Canada to show its concern with the unfortunate of the world's political upheavals. This concern has been demonstrated throughout the post-war years, notably in the displaced persons movement, in connection with the Hungarian uprising, the world refugee year and in other arrangements which have been made for individual refugees with particularly difficult handicaps.
The high commissioner for refugees, as an appointee of the United Nations, deserves our support within the terms of his present mandate. It is the intention of my department- where migration is an appropriate solution- to offer him all possible help within our capabilities. This in itself is not something new but is a reaffirmation of our government's position in the field of refugee problems.
I come now to certain matters of general interest in the immigration field. First, there is the question of legislation. As I mentioned in connection with my visit to the Far East, I am recommending to the governor in council that section 31(c) of the immigration regulations be amended to provide for the addition of male fiances to those categories admissible on the sponsorship of a resident or citizen of Canada. This is all I propose for the moment in this direction. However, it is my firm intention to visit personally, all major areas of immigration operations and from the first hand knowledge which I shall gain, there may well come other recommendations for changes in the legislation.
At the same time, I am conscious of the representations made by members of parliament and others to the effect that there are provisions open to question in certain sections of the present Immigration Act. Some members have introduced private bills with the intention of revising specific sections of the act.
Let me say that I am in sympathy with many of the points raised. However, I think

most members will agree that there are many inter-relationships between various sections of the act, and isolated amendments while perhaps appropriate in respect of one or more particular problems, could have unfortunate effects in other areas.
All the points raised from outside the department as well as from within are being carefully noted and I shall shortly assign priorities for detailed studies of the changes suggested and required. Following this I would expect to introduce a revised act for the consideration of parliament as soon as possible.
Another question of importance in the general policy area is the problem of quality control in the immigration movement. From what I have said earlier I think it should be clear that this government intends to do everything possible to secure, through immigration, a substantial flow of desirable skilled people and their families and to expedite the reunion of families. In this process we intend to improve our administrative facilities and processes to the point where there can be no legitimate excuse for "queue jumping".
While we shall be fair it will be necessary, none the less, to be firm. Persons who seek to circumvent the law by entering Canada illegally, for example, ship deserters, can expect the full process of the law fairly and justly to be applied to them.
At the same time-and with even more emphasis if possible-I should like to stress the government's concern with these elements who seek to infiltrate the Canadian community to carry on criminal activities, especially of the organized variety. Let me assure the committee that persons of the kind under discussion will be denied admission, if known. Those who may have gained admission and are within the jurisdiction of immigration legislation will be subject to the provisions respecting deportation. Obviously all necessary control measures can be effective only with wholehearted public support. I hereby ask for such support from the Canadian people through you, their responsible representatives.
Finally, I am happy to inform the committee that just last night treasury board gave me authority to proceed at once with our plans for reorganization in immigration.
At this time the changes will involve immigration headquarters at Ottawa and our offices overseas. Proposals regarding our offices in Canada will follow in due course. The changes to be made in the organization at the present time will more effectively meet
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the government's policy to implement a more positive and productive immigration program. We shall then have a considerably greater capacity to seek out suitable immigrants, to provide all necessary information about Canada and its opportunities and to speed up the procedures by which immigrants coming either on their own or to join with relatives already in Canada will be dealt with.
Important portions of the work now centralized at Ottawa from our immigration offices in numerous countries will be decentralized in such a way as to eliminate much of the present transfer of paper and the consequent delays. It is important that not only better but that quicker services be given to all those persons who plan to come to this country as immigrants.
The changes in organization should improve the morale of our immigration employees markedly. This is a point the importance of which I have already stressed.
The new organization will reflect fully the functional aspects of the flow of immigration, beginning with its planning, proceeding to the recruitment and selection of immigrants in accord with such planning, and going on to the successful establishment of these immigrants in Canada. There will be five principal divisions at the headquarters in Ottawa: (1) policy and planning; (2) overseas services; (3) Canadian services; (4) special services; and (5) support services. Special services will have to do with those exceptional persons who give unusual difficulty, such as those who must be deported for one reason or another. Support services will have to do with all administrative requirements in respect to finances, personnel, provision of suitable quarters, both in Canada and overseas, furnishings and equipment, and all the numerous basic needs of any large body of employees.
The changes in the plans for the overseas services envisage the setting up of a new regional office in continental Europe, charged with the general supervision of the immigration programs in the 16 countries where we maintain offices. This is comparable in some degree to the regional office we already have in London which covers the United Kingdom and Ireland, but its territory is of course far more extensive and the problems it will meet will be more complex due to the numerous governments with which it will deal and the many languages with which it must have requisite familiarity. The provision of such a regional office at this time
6326	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration will greatly reinforce the efforts of our present offices in the various countries of continental Europe. We will give them much greater support in their promotion and information programs and will be able to react much more quickly and effectively to their requirements than has ever been possible from Ottawa. This is a measure of decentralization that should be most effective. The result should be to stimulate and to expedite Canadian immigration efforts in all the countries now concerned, and in additional countries if such expansion becomes advisable.
In dealing with the reorganization of the overseas immigration services I should point out that these changes are by no means confined to Europe. Another aspect of the new plan will be to so organize as to give added support and attention to the matter of immigrants from sources in the western hemisphere as well as from sources in Asia and in the Pacific areas. For the first time there will be a unit of our immigration staff whose primary responsibility it will be to look after immigration from these important sources.
May I thank the committee for its patience in bearing with me through this fairly lengthy review of a number of important aspects of immigration. I trust it will be helpful to all of us.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to deal with some of the promises that have been made over a period of time as far back as the last election. A promise was made to the Chinese people in my area of Alberta that if they voted Liberal they would not be discriminated against. Promises were made by the former minister of citizenship and immigration that amendments would be brought before the house within a short period of time in respect of the Canadian Citizenship Act and the Immigration Act.
The last time I dealt with this subject was in December of 1963, at which time I referred to several of these promises. At that time the former minister said certain changes were being contemplated. These changes are being contemplated again today.
I should like to quote from the September 24 edition of the Montreal Gazette, as follows:
Sweeping changes to regulations governing the admission to Canada of Chinese immigrants were forecast Monday night by immigration minister Favreau.
Who was the minister trying to impress when he said certain changes were to be made to allow Chinese immigrants into Canada? Perhaps he impressed some of the Chinese people in Canada who were not aware that the important changes had been made by the Conservative minister of citizenship and immigration, Mrs. Ellen Fair-clough. Subsection (c) of section 31 provides for the admission of a somewhat wider list of immediate dependants and close relatives. There were many good things in the minister's statement, but I cannot help expressing my agreement with the hon. member for Edmonton East who said the statement, by and large, was a disappointing one. To me it was something like the old cliche of the curate's egg, good in parts and bad in parts. The total impression was not very satisfactory. The reason I say this to the minister is that despite some of the good points I will mention, and for which he and his department deserve credit, there remains a failure to tackle some of the basic problems, and we will not have a satisfactory immigration policy until they are tackled.
I will deal with that in greater detail later. The announcement as to the proposed changes in the regulations did not deal with the charges which have been made, and properly made, of discrimination written right into the regulations themselves. There is failure to appreciate that right at the root of the procedures laid down at the present time is a system which, as the hon. member for Edmonton East said, perpetuates a disregard for the basic principles of the bill of rights. This has not been dealt with, unfortunately, in the minister's statement.
But may I, first of all, call attention to things in this statement which we welcome. 1 warmly welcome the minister's announcement that steps are to be taken to bring about a positive approach to the subject of immigration. As long as we, or officials in the department, or some of them, think in terms of keeping people out; as long as that is the basic philosophy, no satisfactory result can ever be achieved. I was glad to hear the minister speak of a positive program, and I was glad to hear of the various steps he proposes to take in this direction; the setting up of an interdepartmental committee, for example.
This seems to be an excellent proposal. But why does the hon. gentleman not go a step further? Why do we not have a committee of this house charged with the responsibility of reviewing these matters? I think this parliament should be used. I think there are plenty of people in parliament with experience in these matters who could contribute, not only by making complaints about some of the things which are wrong but, and this is far more important, by helping toward the development of the positive approach of which the minister speaks.
There is one thing which is perfectly obvious. It is that in a sense immigration policy depends upon and is a function of our general over-all economic policy. If we have an


expanding economy there is no problem about getting skilled immigrants to this country. If we have adequate social security measures we do not need to worry about promotional campaigns. Why has there been such a tremendous influx of immigrants into France, Germany and other countries in northern Europe from Italy, Greece and Turkey? No elaborate promotional campaigns were needed. What these countries had were expanding economies and opportunities, and this is a situation which is essential. We can talk as much as we like, but unless there are opportunities available to them, immigrants are not attracted.
The reverse is also true. As long as we have a substantial pool of unemployment in this country the pressure against a liberal immigration policy will be tremendous. It is bound to be so. We have seen it again and again. In times of economic stagnation the minister will be under constant pressure to turn off the tap, to use one of his own expressions; and he certainly has all the means of turning off the tap at his disposal if need be. I welcome this new positive approach and the changes in organization and staffing, both badly needed, which we understand are to be carried out. This approach is useful and worth while, and I wish the minister luck in carrying it out effectively because it is certainly a move in the right direction.
I have no wish to discuss for very long the lengthy passages in his speech in which the minister dealt with the immigration of Chinese from Hong Kong, because I do not regard this as simply a problem involving the Chinese. I regret very much that the only change which is proposed in the regulations should be a minuscule change, namely that females- to adopt the elegant word which was used- can sponsor male fiances, or their entry into this country, whereas hitherto there was apparently discrimination based upon sex. We are all happy to know that this discrimination is to be removed. But if this makes any substantial difference to the situation I shall be surprised. I doubt whether there are enough Chinese females of marriageable age with the ability to attract these young men from Hong Kong to make this change in the regulations more than a tiny gesture.
The minister has, in this instance, frankly stated that he is not recommending that sponsorship privileges for Chinese be extended to cover the admission of brothers, sisters and more distant relatives. That statement, and the regulations which underline it, perpetuate a discrimination which is based, if you like,

on geographical grounds but in reality on racial grounds. It represents the survival in these regulations of racial discrimination.
I have heard the Prime Minister speak on this subject. I have heard the former minister of citizenship and immigration do the same. They together, I imagine, with the present minister, are enlightened men who say they do not have anything to do with discrimination. I remember the Prime Minister speaking heatedly about some United States legislation which continued discrimination on racial grounds. What are the circumstances here? I want the committee to appreciate this. Perhaps the committee does appreciate it already; it is written into the regulations. We do not need to wait for a new session of parliament or for legislation on other items to be completed before we can deal with it. It could be done by order in council with the stroke of a pen. But it is not being done. What is the situation today? Regulation 31(d) states, with application to persons permitted to land in Canada:
a person who is a citizen of any country of Europe, including Turkey; or of any country of North, Central or South America or islands adjacent thereto; or of Egypt, Israel or Lebanon, if such person is:

The minister referred to another matter in rather harsh terms. He spoke of queue jumping. I understand the meaning of queue jumping involves the people coming into this country as visitors, and their desire to stay here and apply for citizenship rather than go back to their country of origin. I appeal to the minister to attempt to find some satisfactory solution to this problem, because section 7, subsection 3 of the Immigration Act itself specifically provides that when a person comes into Canada as a non-immigrant he has a right to report such fact, if he wants to stay, to the nearest immigration officer and present himself for examination at such place and time as may be directed, and that for the purposes under this act, he shall be deemed to be a person seeking admission to Canada.
I am absolutely convinced, Mr. Chairman, that parliament when it enacted that provision intended that if a visitor to Canada for some reason wanted to stay in Canada he should have the right to take his case and have it dealt with in Canada without having to return to his country of origin. I have in mind an individual who, while in Canada, becomes engaged, is offered a job, or who has been a student and, following graduation, desires to stay and work in Canada. I think it was the intention of parliament to give this right to these individuals, provided they are not in a prohibited class, and are qualified for entry.
I understand there is a great problem involved in respect of the machinery of the department, particularly in relation to the admissibility of immigrants. I realize that there are many problems when the department insist on a visitor going through all the requirements following an application for permanent admission. I know it is difficult to carry out the very careful inquiries which must be made, but I feel there must be some solution to these problems.
I would ask hon. members and the minister what would happen if they found themselves in the position of many of these visitors to Canada. I can imagine some of us being unmarried and having a desire to marry someone we met while visiting in another country. If we invited them to Canada as visitors and they decided to live here, how frustrating for the fiancee it would be to have to return to her country of origin and make application for admission to Canada. I can imagine how frustrating it must be for an individual in Canada who met and desired to marry someone from another country, having to send that individual back to the country of origin to make application for citizenship. This is clearly an unsatisfactory situation, and I feel it should be looked into very carefully.
I am wondering whether some method could be found to enable visitors to Canada, who desire to stay, to make application while in this country without having to return to the country of origin. Perhaps the examination carried out in respect of visitors to Canada could be more stringent, but having allowed the visitors in, they should be permitted to make application for citizenship while in Canada. I feel these individuals should have their cases examined as quickly as possible without the necessity of returning to their original homes and making application in the normal manner. After all, I feel it is a compliment to Canada when an individual seeks permission to remain here.
Mr. Chairman, I hope the minister will consider this situation in an attempt to find a solution to this problem, because at the present time the provisions of section 7, subsection 3 of the Immigration Act are being disregarded, and the right that can be conferred by the provisions of that section is not being followed at all.
