Supply-Citizenship and Immigration I think he should seriously consider the remarks that have been made in this house during this debate. I am sure the minister has consulted Mr. Sedgwick, an eminent lawyer from Toronto. I am sure Mr. Sedgwick would tell the minister that many of the procedures now followed are inconsistent with the bill of rights and fundamental principles of justice. I am sure the minister will listen to these remarks and not allow the difficulties and problems that exist to stand in the way of fair and just administration of our immigration laws.
I conclude, Mr. Chairman, by saying that while I commend the minister for his statement, he must go much further than he has to achieve the results required. I hope he has no delusions in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, we appreciate the statement made by the minister in introducing his estimates. I am sure everyone followed with interest the rather lengthy presentation of the immigration picture in Canada today. I must agree with other speakers who have participated in this debate and who have suggested that there was not much indication in his statement of what he intends to do in the future. A great deal of emphasis was placed on plans the department is preparing, but there were no concrete proposals.
I believe this department has a very important role to play in the continued development of Canada. As a nation, Canada has tremendous prospective absorption possibilities. The population of Canada is very limited, being of the order of 19 million. Canada has vast geographic proportions and I feel can absorb a great number of immigrants and can do so very rapidly. I am sure everyone recognizes the necessity of increasing our population in order to develop markets adequate to absorb our production. There is a great deal of emphasis placed on overseas markets. We must dispose of our produce. I am sure we can do so by creating larger markets within our own borders. I think our domestic markets would grow following the adoption of the suggested new immigration policy, allowing people into Canada who will accept the responsibilities as well as the privileges of citizenship in this great country of ours.
The minister outlined the steps he proposed to take to improve immigration facilities. He referred to an interdepartmental committee as being a method of meeting the needs and demands in this respect. I think this is a very good suggestion and will help to alleviate the poor situation now in existence.


I think one of the most important things to do in respect of the promotional campaign he mentioned, is to develop this country, and by practical steps to show other people exactly what Canada is and what it can become. This cannot be done through the use of propaganda. We in this country do know of our vast resources and productive capacity. I am sure we can achieve a greater degree of development and progress than has been achieved to the present time. I am sure one of the ways of doing this is by bringing people into this country who will develop the nation as quickly as possible. I think when this development has taken place the example will be obvious to all countries of the world.
Not only must there be adequate policies in respect of immigration, the policies must be co-ordinated with those of every government department. I do not think it is possible for the minister and his department alone to do the job which must be done. As I pointed out before, there is a tremendous amount of development and progress needed to achieve the desired results. I feel there must be a correlation of policies of all departments in order to bring this about. Generally speaking I have found the officials of the immigration branch quite co-operative with regard to the matters I have discussed with them, but I believe that in many instances they are hampered by legislation and regulations that are in the main too restrictive in their nature. This has been referred to by the speakers who have preceded me. 1 am not going to labour the point but I believe there must be an opening up, a liberalization of the legislation and rules and regulations in order to make them more effective and to do the job that we believe the immigration department should do in this particular field.
The minister dealt mainly with immigration. I realize that this is a very important phase of his departmental responsibilities, but I believe that attention should be given to the requirements, privileges and responsibilities of Canadian citizenship. It is not sufficient just to bring people into Canada. It is not sufficient just to encourage them to come here and take up residence within our nation. I believe that the responsibilities of citizenship should be impressed upon them. In this regard I refer not only to new immigrants. I believe that all the people of Canada should realize that in accepting the privileges and benefits that are theirs within the borders of our country they must also be prepared to accept the responsibilities of citizenship. I have

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
raised this matter before and I believe it is a subject which should receive a great deal more consideration than it has up to the present time.
In making his statement the minister indicated he was not going to refer at this time to his responsibilities with respect to Indian affairs but would reserve his statement on that matter until we come to that branch. I believe that is desirable and makes for more effective debate.
Extensive debate has already taken place on interim supply motions with regard to immigration, and our participation in the debate at this time is going to be very limited. However there is one other point to which I should like to refer. The minister mentioned revision of the act. It would appear that this is highly desirable not only for the purpose of making the necessary changes that are required but also for the purpose of making the whole act more readable and more understandable and in that way making it more effective in accomplishing the particular task.
We would urge the minister to continue his diligent attention to these particular fields. I think it is absolutely essential to remember that especially in this department the human factor is of primary importance.

Mr. Chairman, in speaking on the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration I do not want to take a lot of time. I was very glad to hear the minister state that the policy of the department is going to be a positive rather than a negative one and that we are actively going out to seek new immigrants for this country. Too often in the past I have felt that the department-when I say "department" I mean a combination of the legislation, the regulations and the department itself-has tended to act not as a pump drawing people into our country but more as a wall trying to keep them out. I hope and expect from the minister's statement that this will end.
There are three specific items that have been touched on about which I should like to make a few remarks. First of all, the hon. member for Greenwood raised the problem of geographic and racial discrimination in our immigration policy. I can only agree with him that I think this is wrong. I believe this is something that is not in keeping with the image of our country we want to present abroad and I do not think it is in keeping with the view of our attitudes that we ourselves have within our country. So I would ask the minister to regard this problem as a problem, and see if something cannot be
done about it. I say again that the arguments presented by the hon. member for Greenwood made a lot of sense to me and I would hope that consideration might be given to them.
The second problem I should like to speak about briefly is that of immigrants from behind the iron curtain. As I understand the regulations, people within a certain age group are not admitted to this country because we are unable to find out anything about them. We do not know whether they are acceptable from a security point of view. It seems to me that because we are unable to prove the case for admission of these people we are in a position of having to assume the case against. We cannot prove they are fit immigrants for the country so we say that they must be unfit.
I am fully aware of the security problems involved. On the other hand, I do think there is something that might be done which has not been done in the past. Instead of looking only to the immigrant himself as a source of information about his character I think we might look to this end of the story. We might look to the sort of people who are sponsoring the immigrant. If we are going to bring somebody from behind the iron curtain to this country, and the people who are sponsoring him, the family with whom he is going to live, are people of good character and of industry who have established themselves as good citizens of this country, surely we should be able to give some consideration to the risk involved in bringing a person into that environment. If we have confidence, as I do, in our system of life in this country I think we should not be afraid of bringing somebody who might possibly be a communist into this type of environment, in the hope that our system would commend itself to the immigrant. So I would urge the department to look at the problem not only from the point of view of trying to find out information about the prospective immigrant in ^ his country of origin but also from the point of view of the environment here to which the immigrant is coming, and see if we cannot establish some yardsticks on that basis that might allow some of these people into the country, that might allow some family reunions which, based on the experience of the cases I have had, I think should take place.
The third point I should like to raise deals with the problem of mental illness. This is the subject of a private member's bill which I have on the order paper, but the way the schedule is going I do not think there is a
6836	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration chance that the bill will come up for debate this session. It was on the order paper last session but did not come up then either.
I think the easiest way for me to describe this problem is to cite the case history that first brought the problem to my attention. I refer to the case of a man who during the war lost his family and wandered throughout war torn Europe. After the war he was able to obtain certain skills as an electrician and became engaged to be married to a girl. His engagement was broken and he came to Canada in 1953. Shortly after he arrived in this country he had a nervous or mental breakdown and went into a mental hospital. There he stayed for a period of a couple of months, I believe. Since that time this man has established himself in this country. He has worked steadily since 1953, a period of 11 years now, and there has been absolutely no problem at all in terms of his mental health. He has had recent examinations by psychiatrists and they have indicated that his previous problem was the result of the upbringing he had during the war, the breaking up of his family, the loss of his parents, the breaking of his engagement and then suddenly being transplanted to this environment. The pressures were too great. But since that time he has re-established himself and from current psychiatric examinations the indications are that he is probably as good or a better risk than most people in this country today. This man is under an order of deportation.
Now, it is true this order of deportation will not be exercised. Indeed it cannot be exercised because there is no place we can send him. He is now a resident of Canada. It is fine to say to the man: You do not have to worry; you can stay here all the rest of your life. The order of deportation will not he exercised. This may seem like a reasonable thing to say. However in my opinion it is not. This man cannot become a Canadian citizen or become the citizen of any country. He cannot get a passport as you and I can to visit other countries. He is denied many of the rights that we, as Canadians, have. He is denied these rights under the Immigration Act, and not just for today or tomorrow; he is denied them all the rest of his life.
He wants to get married and raise a family. However he refuses to do so under these circumstances. He does not want to bring up children and have to try to explain to those children why he cannot go to Europe like other Canadians, or hold a passport from

this country. I do not believe this is good enough. I believe that the legislation, as it is drafted now, fails to take into account the advancements that have been made in connection with the problem of mental illness. It fails to recognize what all other institutions in our society seem to recognize, that is that mental illness can be cured. We allow a prisoner who has been in our prisons, but who has rehabilitated himself, to become a Canadian citizen. I believe we should do the same thing for people who have been unfortunate enough to have had mental problems. I think we should recognize that these people can be cured, and after adequate proof of cure I think we should then return them to full status as Canadians. I believe that to do less is not in keeping with our attitudes in this country. I urge the minister, when he is making his revision of the Immigration Act, to bring this section up to date because in my opinion it is almost reminiscent of the middle ages. A change should be made so that a mental patient receives proper treatment in this country.

I wish to associate myself, Mr. Chairman, with the remarks of the previous speaker, who made some very good suggestions. I hope the minister takes note of them. I wish to congratulate particularly the hon. member for Edmonton East for his remarks because when we are considering the extension of immigration quotas for people from other lands, I believe the department would be well advised to co-operate more fully with the Department of Industry so these people can make use of their skills when they arrive in Canada.
My remarks I hope will be brief because I intend to refer to that branch of the department which has responsibility for the Indian population in Canada. The minister's introductory remarks were quite extensive and he should be complimented. He covered a great deal of territory. We find champions for almost everything in Canada. We find people who champion the cause of law breakers, people who come into Canada illegally. We are so careful, and we want to give them free legal advice and see they are comfortably housed in our prisons. We want to see that they get the proper bail. We have champions for those who deliberately take the life of another. Just a short time ago an organization was established in Canada to lobby for the abolition of capital punishment. Canada sends a great deal of money to the underdeveloped nations through the Colombo plan.

Who does champion the cause of the Indians? We have almost a quarter of a million of these people in Canada. There was a time when we thought they were faced with extinction. However the Indian population is increasing and we have them in every province. I have some in my constituency, approximately 1,300 men, women and children scattered over five reserves. It is with these people I am familiar, but I think the same situation exists in every part of Canada in so far as our Indians are concerned.
I was particularly intrigued by a centennial project initiated by the Saskatchewan wheat pool, Mr. Chairman, and I wish to make a short reference to it. The Saskatchewan wheat pool has initiated what they call a conference and trade centre to be built in Saskatoon. The federal-provincial contribution will be $92,000 and public contributions will amount to around $150,000. This building is for the purpose of teaching the Indians in order to bridge the gap between the different cultures, thus enabling these Indians to lead a richer life. These short courses are going to be five or ten days, or perhaps of two weeks duration and will be given to Indians of all ages. The Saskatchewan wheat pool is to be commended for initiating such a project. I fail to see why this example could not be followed up by the government, instead of neglecting this section of our population as we do.
Now, Mr. Chairman, these are first Canadians. Away back almost 500 years ago when the first white man came to this country, the Indians had a culture. They had reached a certain level of civilization. They did not have a common language but they had an organized government and some ideas for practising democracy. One does not need to stretch his imagination too far to visualize what would have happened if the white man had not come and this Indian population, simply by a process of evolution, had been allowed to progress culturally. One wonders if these people would not have reached, by this time, a much higher level than some of the multitribal nations in Africa. I have great respect for the intelligence of these people. However, today they have no ambition. I think we have destroyed that.
What have we given the Indian? We have put him in a reserve, in a ghetto. We have destroyed his pride of race. We have destroyed his initiative. We have destroyed his ambition to do better because all we hand out to him is a relief voucher. He lives from day to day because he knows the little white
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration father, the government, is going to take care of him. I admit that the schools on the various reserves are trying to do a good job. I commend the department for having started an experiment several years ago, namely encouraging the integration of the Indian boys and girls into our public school system.
I speak from experience because from one large Indian reserve in my riding a number of children were brought into our public schools, and from the conversations I have had with the board of trustees and the teachers, I learn they are making satisfactory progress. This experiment should be extended to the full. We should do away with the idea of the one room school on the Indian reserve where at times it is most difficult to secure a qualified teacher.
Some of the residential schools are also doing a wonderful job, and in my constituency the Birtle residential school is doing a magnificent job. We must achieve integration for the Indians. We must destroy any suspicions we have had. We must restore the Indian's confidence in himself so that when he gets education he may qualify for better positions. Educated Indians will become leaders in their communities, and I believe the project which the Saskatchewan wheat pool has initiated is a good one, which could be copied by many other parts of Canada.
Indian affairs are in no way related to citizenship and immigration. Citizenship and immigration are two subjects, related to each other, and I would suggest that the government give consideration to establishing an Indian affairs department. It might be created by providing for an associate minister of citizenship and immigration who would give his full time to Indian affairs.
Indian reserves are scattered all over the nation. Suggestions have been made that they be abolished, and the Indians have gone up in arms over those suggestions. Outside of striving to integrate some of the young we are not doing a thing to encourage Indians to establish themselves on the land that is presently cultivated by the whites. There are thousands of acres of good arable farmland rented by white farmers, on an acreage fee or on a share basis. Is it not about time we took steps to prepare the Indians to take over this land? It is their land, and if they worked it it would put an end to the spectacle of Indians waiting for relief vouchers.
An associate minister of Indian affairs would assist the minister greatly. At present the department is too big for one man to handle. It is a troika, as Khrushchev would
6838	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration say, and in no way are Indians connected with citizenship and immigration. They do not have to be naturalized; they are the first citizens of this nation.
Several years ago, probably intended as an experiment and on the recommendation of the departmental heads, a change was made by taking the Indian agent off the reserve and putting him as far away as possible, presumably with the idea of encouraging the Indian to be self-supporting and to depend on himself and his band. In some instances in my riding the Indian agent is 40 or 50 miles away from the reserve to which he is assigned. In fact the nearest agent to a reserve is 50 miles away. The Indian has been in the habit of coming to the agent and regarding him as a father confessor, telling the agent all his problems, grievances and beefs. I know it is not pleasant for an Indian agent to live on a reserve ostracized from white society, but this is one of the hazards of his job, and I feel he should be as close as possible to the reserve, if not actually on it.
The Indian never goes anywhere without dragging his family along with him. You will see an Indian and his wife sitting on the roadside trying to hitchhike a ride to see the Indian agent. If they can afford the bus fare they travel that way, but the agent should be nearer to them.
I do not know what qualifications are expected of Indian agents. I am not offering any criticism of any agent I know personally, but I believe the agent has to be a teacher. He should also be an agricultural expert so that he may encourage Indians to make use of the land on which they reside. By competition he should instil in the Indian ambition to own, to possess something, rather than be content to carry on day by day without any hope for the future.
We have to have more houses on Indian reserves. If we have millions of dollars to spend for everything else then we must also have them for these people. We have put these people on reserves, and you should see the conditions under which many of them live. We worry about what is going on in Malaysia and Africa; I say let us start worrying about what is going on at our own back door or front door. Surely we can give better dwellings to the Indians, many of whom are living in hovels, log cabins with barely a covering on them, with broken window panes and bad floors. These are a blot on our civilization.
Let us try to integrate the Indians into our way of life. Let us get them into our

public schools. Let us put dedicated Indian agents on our reserves. Let us bring the Indian to a level where he does not suffer from an inferiority complex. If that is done the department will be accomplishing something. I hope the minister will keep some of these suggestions in mind. They are important, and this is a segment of our population which we must attend to if we want to present a respectable face to the rest of the world.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few brief comments on a subject which we are too often inclined to treat lightly, whereas it is the most essential subject to be found in this country, and I refer to immigration in so far as it relates to the demographic composition of Canada.
In accordance with our best traditions and by way of introduction, I should like to begin by congratulating the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, of whom we have reason to be proud.
Not too long ago, I had the opportunity to witness one of his performances on television, when he faced a panel of interviewers who stuck to their guns rather hard, and I was able to see how masterfully he handled their questions, which is altogether in keeping with his great ability and exceptional talent.
Hear, hear.

I am pleased to hear the applause of my colleagues, because what I have to say later on might not meet with their approval.
The immigration problem is surely one of the most difficult for French Canada. It is obvious that our country can admit a very great number of immigrants, but it is also obvious, unfortunately, that immigration has never favoured the French speaking group. Figures are there to prove it.
I put on the order paper several questions regarding immigration, in order to learn how many immigrants have been admitted and have settled here since the beginning of the century. In those questions I was asking for the number of French speaking and English speaking Canadians; this would definitely show that the French speaking element has been reduced, through immigration, to a very alarming extent.
We believe in the dual language character of our country. Many people say that they want to accept the bilingual and bicultural fact. We probably find this good will every-

where, but even if those high-sounding principles were broadcast from coast to coast, from Newfoundland to British Columbia, if
the French speaking element is constantly losing ground in Canada from a demographic point of view, the day will come when it will be absolutely useless to speak of bilingualism or biculturalism, for there will no longer be any French speaking element.
Then I shall appeal to any Canadian citizen to come to our assistance in the province of Quebec, in order to fight those who exploit prejudice and those who would like to drive our compatriots into breaking up our confederation. We are able to face up with the utmost energy and courage to those who resort to prejudice, but we want also to provide them with acceptable arguments in order to prove to them that confederation is to our advantage and not to our disadvantage, as they try to make us believe by foul and surreptitious means.
Mr. Chairman, the facts show that: Since 1946, Canada has welcomed 2,200,000 immigrants, of whom 650,000 were British, 270,000 German, 320,000 Italian, 160,000 Dutch, etc. and as far as the French speaking immigrants are concerned, they numbered fewer than 70,000.
It is clear that in the circumstances, a large proportion of immigrants is drawn to the majority group and inclined to identify itself with, and become part of that group, for which they can hardly be blamed.
But the point I would like to submit, Mr. Chairman, is that to the extent the French minorities in the nine other provinces are strengthened, become strong and actively dynamic, we shall be able, not only to fight, but to eliminate separatists, by telling them: If Quebec should separate there would still be a strong French speaking minority to denounce them as traitors and renegades. But, if the French speaking minorities in the remainder of this country are inexistent, the separatists will then gain the support of those who are weak enough to yield to their arguments.
My impression is that if we really want to establish a biethnic country, I think the area where this principle should be confirmed is the Immigration Act, where the demographic balance could be considered in one way or the other.
It is by laying down that biethnical principle, by recognizing it in the Immigration Act, that we will assert ourselves. And that, all the much more if it is recognized that
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration bilingualism and biculturalism prevail in this country.
I would be remiss if I failed to deplore the lack of interest shown by the government of the province of Quebec in regard to immigration. That government was at fault, altogether. Certainly, such a lack of interest is consistent with the theories expressed not too long ago by the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) who seemed to be afraid of the fact that Algerian immigrants were to settle in the province of Quebec. It is because of such obsolete and out of date prejudices that we have continually lost ground as far as immigration is concerned.
I have here a booklet written by Jean-Marc Leger, who is particularly interested in the problems of immigration and he wrote this:
But there is a general complaint and also a general surprise: "French Canadians always speak to us in English. Even when we address them in French, if they detect a foreign accent or a certain slowness of speech, they immediately switch to English.
Here I speak on behalf of the immigrants who come to Canada and are surprised to see that as soon as French speaking Canadians realize that their name has a foreign sound they have a tendency to speak to them in English.
French Canadians show a lot of thoughtlessness which should be remedied if we want our grievances to be justified and accepted.
And Mr. Leger continues:
In other circumstances, our people will consider new Canadians as English speaking people when it comes to the distribution of pamphlets or booklets published in French and in English. In a hotel or on a streetcar, in a restaurant or in a store, the name or the accent of a new Canadian will immediately encourage the French Canadian employee to carry the conversation in English.
The situation is so ridiculous that some of our fellow citizens speak in English to French immigrants with Basque or Alsatian names.
And Mr. Leger said further that this xenophobia has always existed among a great number of us and, as a result, the immigrant did not feel at home when he came to live in Quebec.
It is on account of speeches such as those delivered by a former minister of the crown that immigrants are reluctant to come and live in Canada and more especially in the province of Quebec. It is on account of that backward attitude that immigration has always been unfavourable to French Canada.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks. If we really want Quebec to develop within confederation, the dual language principle should definitely be
6840	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration included in the Immigration Act in one way or another.
Second, I think we would be justified in asking that the demographic balance, which was momentarily upset following massive immigration into Canada since the turn of the century, be corrected in some way so that the French minorities, as I was saying a moment ago, be strengthened numerically in the English speaking provinces. Then we would be in a position to say to the Quebec separatists: you have people in the other provinces who are speaking your language and have your culture and with whom we must make common cause in order to become true Canadians worthy of the name.
Mr. Chairman, could I ask a question of the hon. member for Lotbiniere? [Translation]
If my hon. colleague will be kind enough to let me complete my remarks, then he may ask questions.
I would like to ask the hon. member-

I will answer your question at the end of my remarks.
Mr. Chairman, may I submit a third suggestion? I wonder if it would be so unpleasant to consider the following possibility: the law requires that when an immigrant becomes a naturalized Canadian, he must have a sufficient knowledge of one of the two official languages in Canada. Would it be so unreasonable to demand that a part from a sufficient knowledge of one of the two official languages in this country, the immigrant should also have a basic knowledge of the second official language in Canada, because after all when he has been living for five years in a bietihnical and bicultural country, it seems to me that he should have an idea of the second culture and the second official language of that country.
And as a fourth suggestion-I do not know whether this would meet completely the ideas of the minister-I have the impression that the demographic make-up in a country is so primordial and vital that I feel we should have a parliamentary committee on immigration. This is a personal opinion that I am voicing-

Mr. Chairman, I am happy that this intervention of my hon. colleague


from Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) takes place now because I think he will cry out even more when he hears my fifth suggestion.
I belong to the younger generation, and we consider ourselves essentially Canadian everywhere; we respect the feelings and the principles of the older and more experienced generation who believes in ties and symbols which to our minds, are the badge of colonialism.
I believe that we of the younger generation must respect the feelings of the older generation but our generation must not be accused of being revolutionary because it wants to eliminate all colonialism symbols. We want our country to be essentially Canadian. There is a provision in the Immigration Act whereby every Canadian citizen is a British subject. I recognize that that may please a great number of Canadians, but you cannot blame the young people of my generation if they believe that the fact that we are subjects of another country constitutes a tie of bondage of one country to the other. In my opinion, we should be essentially Canadian, Canadian citizens, and if we want to pay respect to the crown presiding over the commonwealth, why could not all commonwealth nations grant mutual citizenship instead of giving recognition by legislation to a tie of servitude?

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few remarks regarding education among our Indian youth. A most outstanding development of school administration in recent years has been the enrolment of native children into non-Indian schools. Last year this trend affected 36 per cent of more than
50,000	young people from the reserves. This required 157 joint school agreements with provincial and local authorities-an excellent example of federal-provincial co-operation in providing an important community service. However, I would remind the minister that the Glassco commission recommended "the more rapid development of school integration as worthy of top priority". I hope the appropriate authorities will act on this advice and encourage an increasing number of families to send their children to non-Indian schools.
Last year a delegation from British Columbia presented a brief to the government in which they urged "a stepped up program of vocational training for native boys and girls with spot centres in Indian districts". Facilities of this kind would provide training that would prepare young people for job opportunities that are now closed to them. This would do much to lessen the possibility of discrimination in the field of employment. Such a development would take place more generally with the building of more and more technical and vocational institutions across the country.
School drop-outs among Indian youth at the secondary school level across Canada can be described only as a tragedy. In 1960 according to government reports only 82 students were doing work beyond grade 12. Last year only 98 of our native population were in attendance at a Canadian university.
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
Every effort should be made to encourage more bright young Indian students to take advantage of the scholarships and other forms of assistance that are available at the present time. I hope Professor Hawthorne and his associates will conduct a searching inquiry to discover the reasons for the excessively large number of drop-outs among native children in the secondary schools across Canada. This country needs the services of more educated young Indian boys and girls in industry, in business and in the public service.
The department is to be commended for its program in the field of adult education. Last year 2,061 men and women were enrolled in a variety of courses, many of the instructors being provided by the extension departments of the universities. This is excellent work in citizenship and occupational training and should be encouraged in every way. However the adult education program is handicapped by lack of native Indian teachers. More of these young people should be persuaded to enrol in teacher training institutions. At present there are 1,500 teachers in Indian schools but only 200 are natives themselves.
Finally may I urge greater attention to setting up more Indian friendship or social centres in thickly populated areas across Canada. Eleven cities have such meeting places now, as a result of the interest and initiative of local groups. Vancouver recently commenced a service of this kind through the action of enterprising citizens and local native people themselves. But they are having financial difficulties.
To an annual budget of $18,000, the department of indian affairs contributes only $5,000. I understand that this is the maximum amount paid to any of the centres in Canada. Mr. Chairman, I should like to state that there are several Indian reservations in my constituency. Many of the Indians have asked to have the reservations enlarged. I think this could be very well avoided and that the first question should be as to your national status. Instead of inquiring about the place and date of your birth they should inquire about your citizenship and should not be concerned with where you were born and how you were born. Mr. Chairman, I should like to touch briefly on a matter which I feel is of great concern to the people of Canada and has to do with immigration. I refer to the case of Mr. Harold Banks. I do not intend to rehash previous arguments about this man nor do I intend to express my opinion of the illegal action of the Liberal government which gave this man the status of a landed immigrant in Canada. But I should like to suggest a way that may free us of this man entirely.

I believe many people are unaware that when the previous government was in office the former minister of citizenship and immigration, Hon. Ellen Fairclough, refused to grant Mr. Banks citizenship. She did everything in her power to rectify the action of the previous government which had granted him landed status.
I believe that under the Immigration Act a landed immigrant who leaves Canada with the intention of living permanently outside of Canada loses the domicile he has attained, whether he has been in Canada one or ten years. I am not a lawyer and therefore cannot give a legal opinion, but I would think that if Mr. Banks is a fugitive from justice, if he has fled from Canada to the United States to avoid serving the 30 day sentence imposed upon him for contempt of court, this might easily be construed as leaving Canada with the intention of remaining permanently outside this country.
I suggest that the present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration should look into this matter most carefully. If Mr. Banks has indeed left the country and lost his domicile by so doing, then every effort should be made to ensure that if and when he applies for reentry into Canada he be required to meet every test applied to all immigrants coming here for the first time. If these tests are properly applied, I am sure he can be refused entry as a person convicted of crimes involving moral turpitude under section 5(d) of the Immigration Act.
Then there is also the Hooper case, the man who was detained in Don jail for 100 days because he refused to answer questions that were asked by an immigration officer. It is true that under a certain section of the Immigration Act an officer has the power to detain and that it is an offence to refuse to answer questions. However the act was passed long before the passage of the bill of rights, which guarantees certain freedoms. Is it in the spirit of the bill of rights to hold a club of possible imprisonment over the head of a man who refuses to testify against himself? Should a person suspected of being in this country illegally be forced to provide evidence on which his deportation can be ordered? Should not the same principle apply as applies in any other prosecution? The civil police must build up their own case against an accused. There is no provision in the Criminal Code as far as I know whereby a person can be jailed for failing to make a confession.

Some people have suggested to me that so far as immigration is concerned they do not feel that the government is pursuing a sufficiently aggressive policy to bring immigrants into this country who are prepared to do manual work. I refer particularly to the field of agriculture, including gardeners, caretakers and manual workers. A great many fail on the tests of skills imposed by the department which are perhaps too severe under present conditions. Perhaps a plan along the lines suggested by some of the experts along those lines to bring in people from some countries who will do the manual jobs should be initiated by the minister of immigration.
I want to refer to the immigrants who have built up this country and to say first of all that actually the only citizens of this country are the North American or red Indians. All the rest of us are immigrants. The first immigrants, of course, were the French. They were followed by people from the United Kingdom. Then the United Empire Loyalists came to this country and they were composed of Germans as well as those of English stock. Then followed immigrants from the British Isles and then European immigrants in the main, until today in this country we have a million people of German descent, half a million Ukrainians, half a million Nether-landers, half a million Italians and many others totalling in all three million. The result is that today we have a country of minorities.
But I want to say that we cannot just thank federal governments for the policies of immigration and methods of bringing people into the country that have been initiated. I remember that in 1945 no move at all was being made to bring immigrants into the country and Hon. George Drew, who was premier of Ontario at that time, started an airlift. Within the space of a few months he brought in approximately 25,000 people. This demonstrated to the federal government that they would have to get off their seats and start moving.
Over the years since 1945 over 2i million immigrants have come to our shores and the province of Ontario from which I come has taken over half of them. Many of these immigrants who have come to Canada over the years have made substantial contributions to our economy. Names come to my mind such as Stephen Roman of Denison Consolidated, Romandale Farms and other enterprises. I think of the great contribution made by Mr. Koerner of British Columbia who established

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration sawmills throughout that province and finally-created the Koerner foundation which has done so much to help the University of British Columbia and education generally in that province. Then there is the Bata firm from Czechoslovakia which founded a town in Ontario and established one of the great shoe factories in Canada. I think too of the Bick family who came from Holland. Mr. Bick came here as a market gardener in a modest way and gradually expanded his enterprises until he went into pickle manufacturing and is now one of the big pickle manufacturers on this continent.
Then, in so far as the farm sector is concerned, since 1945 immigrants have purchased lands worth over $100 million. I want to say, Mr. Chairman, that some of these farms would be abandoned today if it were not for these immigrants. Agriculture needs workers because of the older age group-in this industry.
It is in the professional field that I am particularly concerned. There were over
100,000	professional people who entered Canada since the war. Of these, 20,000 were engineers. I sometimes wonder if we stop to think of the great contribution these immigrants make in dollars and cents, to say nothing of their brain power. The cost of educating these 20,000 engineers at about $6,000 each would be over $120 million, to say nothing of the cost of raising them until they were ready to enter university. These people come over here ready to go to work and their earning capacity represents well over a quarter of a million dollars each. This is a great economic thrust to our economy.
I should like to speak for a moment about my own profession. There were 6,000 doctors entering Canada since 1945, most of whom came from the British Isles. The cost of training these 6,000 doctors would be approximately $84 million in Canada. This is a gift. I am not including the cost of raising these doctors from infancy until the time they were ready to go to medical school. The earning power of this group would be approximately $3 billion, quite a proportion of which would go to the government in the form of income taxes. It is a fact that since the last war 37 per cent of all the doctors in this country, including our own medical school graduates, came from outside of this country. About 18,000 of the nurses who are today working in the hospitals across Canada were trained in hospitals outside of this country. Think of what it would have cost us to have raised these young people from birth
[Mr. Rynard.l

and then trained them to take their place in the world.
Then, I come to the other professional fields. We find that over 16,000 teachers and professors have come to this country since 1945. We are very short, as I have said, of doctors and nurses at the moment. The Hall commission report stressed the need for doctors and nurses over the next 10 years and the need for five new medical schools, as I pointed out before. The shortage will become more acute because the sources of supply overseas are drying up. It takes something like seven years to train a doctor from the time he starts medical school until he is ready to go to work. No drive has been needed up to this moment in order to attract doctors to this country. As a matter of fact, the government of the day deserves no credit, in many ways, for the people who have come here. We have to change our tactics. Doctors are harder to get. I would suggest to the government that they consider offering some incentives to the medical profession. Certainly, positions should be located. There will be difficulty in getting the doctors. However, the government should hold consultations with the Canadian medical association to ascertain the best way of attracting these doctors when they reach our shores. I am thinking of the first six months or the first year they are here when they have to pass examinations. Perhaps some degree of latitude could be given in these particular fields. These doctors are well trained, most of them in United Kingdom universities. I draw to the attention of the minister the fact that this matter is urgent. We will be unable to turn out sufficient doctors from our own medical schools for the next 10 years.
When I say the need is urgent, Mr. Chairman, all I have to do is to point out to you that there are hospitals across Canada today that are operating without interns. I can go to the metropolitan city of Toronto and indicate hospitals which are running without interns. I can take you to hospitals where there are floors closed because we have not the nursing personnel to run them. This is not good enough. I say to the minister therefore that he should get in touch with the Canadian medical association to see what can be done to bring to this country physicians, nurses and trained personnel.

I do not intend to spend a great deal of time on these estimates today because the two questions I want to raise have been discussed during this session and the last session of parliament. First of all, I was in-

terested in the remarks made by the minister concerning the attitude of the Canadian government toward immigrants from Hong Kong. The minister made one or two statements which I believe appeared to indicate a changed attitude toward the immigration problem in Hong Kong.

I now wish to refer to a particular case in my constituency, but I shall not name the individual concerned. I shall send the name to the minister. This man has resided in Canada for 35 years, and although on four occasions a judge has passed his application 20220-433
for citizenship it was turned down by ministerial authority. This man has now made his fifth application and he sincerely and honestly does not know what caused the rejection of his previous ones.

From talking to his neighbours I am satisfied there must be something in his file that has no foundation. I hope the estimates of the department will pass quickly, Mr. Chairman, but I do feel I should say a few words with regard to immigration because of the importance of the subject to my riding and Canada as a whole. In St. Paul's riding about one third of the residents are people who have made their homes there after coming from other countries. The great majority of them have become good Canadian citizens, and have made a great contribution to the life of Toronto and to the riding itself. Therefore I have a particular interest in immigration because of the nature of my riding, and also I have a particular interest in it because I have served as a member of the United Church committee on immigration, which is concerned with questions relating to this department.
I was delighted to hear the minister say he proposed to adopt a positive program to welcome immigrants to Canada. This is about the most important decision that any minister of immigration could make. I welcome that statement. I believe immigrants should not

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration be treated as people who are looking for favours when they ask for admission to Canada. They should not be treated as suppliants. They should be welcomed to this country and treated with respect, and that attitude should prevail no matter what the colour of their skin, no matter what their country of origin, no matter what their level of education. I am delighted to know that is the approach which the minister proposes to adopt.
There was one point, however, in the minister's remarks which caused me some concern and which I would ask him to review very carefully with his departmental officials. I refer to the statement on page 13 of the speech notes in which the minister indicated that the Chinese amnesty program might be changed in some way-
He said "suspended", "terminated".

Mr. Chairman, I just wish to make a few remarks at this time which will hasten the passage of the estimates item by item, because I am not holding up any item. First of all, this is my first opportunity to congratulate the minister on his appointment. Coupled with that I would like to congratulate his parliamentary secretary, because he is a man for whom during the time I have been in the house I have had great personal respect. I have had fine cooperation from the minister personally, and his parliamentary secretary, in the cases I have brought to their attention, although I have not always had satisfactory conclusions. However, I think I can go this far and say that the minister personally exhibits those traits of character and non-prejudice which I think are very important in holding the office that he does.
I think that is about as far as I can go in congratulating him on his effort today. After


reading his speech-which I was very happy to receive, incidentally, and give attention to -which is to be reproduced outside the house, and considering the promises of the Liberal party to the electorate, I agree with the hon. member for Greenwood who said we had only a mouse in the literature in front of us. Why it was felt that this speech contained so much and was important enough to warrant prior release to the press gallery, for the life of me I cannot understand, in view of the election promises that were made and the Liberal planks in this regard which brought them support-for I believe these planks and promises did bring them support.
There is no evidence here of any priority and I do not know why this government places priorities on certain things which seem to have very little importance when one considers the major problems of Canada, and at the same time probably frustrate the minister in his desires to carry out his own personal wishes in amending this legislation. I think the Canadian people deserve an explanation of these things.
I agree generally with the remarks that have been made throughout this debate. I fully agree with the remarks of the hon. member who has just resumed his seat. I am concerned with one announcement in this presentation of the minister to the committee, namely that the amnesty and adjustment program will be terminated on September 1. First of all I would like to suggest to the minister that it is unfair to a large segment of the people, because the immigration offices have not been able to handle the work that has come to them through this program. It is the experience at my local office that the people who seek to make statements have sometimes had to wait two or three weeks before anything is done. Perhaps this has been because an interpreter was needed, but sometimes it has been because the business of the office was so heavy that the officials could not attend to the particular case. That is one reason why I think the announcement that this program will terminate two weeks from now is a terrible one, and I urge the minister to reconsider this matter. I am going to make some suggestions to him in this regard before I conclude my remarks.
The other matter I want to emphasize today-and I know from speaking personally to the minister that he is aware of this situation-is that although they say the program is four years old and this has been ample time for everyone to take advantage of it, this is not in truth the fact. First of all, it

was a year to a year and a half, or maybe two years, before there was any co-operation from the Chinese community in regard to this program. There is a very basic and a very good reason for this. These people are a law unto themselves. Although they render services to the communities in which they live and to all people who can bring them business, in their own personal relationships they are very, very close and there is a very definite authority in the head of a Chinese family.
In many cases the head of the Chinese family is 70 or 75 years old. He is a small fellow who has probably been afraid all his life. He knows what the circumstances are in respect of his status and is afraid of the result of any disclosure on his part. Very often this man has worked all his life, made a success of a small business and has supported a family. What does happen as a result of the police disclosure and action? I am sure we all know the answer to that question.
Very often the head of the family has been frightened by stories told him by the individuals who make money out of these situations. The Chinese fellow is afraid he will lose his position and be sent out of the country. He has often told his own family what to say about their regularization status. False information is given by all the members of his family.
Young Chinese people refer to their fathers as "daddy". Some of these young children have told me that their parents told them to give the false information they have been giving. Many times these people will not give explanations at all. I have one particular situation in mind. A Chinese family has been running a grocery and has found a good living in this occupation from the point of view of their requirements. There is one son in this family who in fact is an illegal entrant. This husband and wife did not have any children of their own. The father before bringing his wife to Canada made three trips to China. When his wife came to Canada they followed an old Chinese custom and brought this boy as their son. He was not in fact a blood son.
I spent a good deal of time with these people over a period of three years. I have known the family for some 20 years. On each occasion I visited them they would say: "You help our son; you help our son". I said: "Pop, I want to help you". On each occasion they would tell me a slightly different story. After the three year period I had decided in my own mind what the discrepancies and untruths were. I finally paid a visit to this
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration family and told the son there was nothing I would rather do than help him obtain a regularized status. I said to him, "You are not telling me the truth. I have come to four or five conclusions about what you have told me. Many things you have said are not true." I then told him what I felt was the truth. The young lad then said, "You are almost right, Mr. More, but what I have told you is what my daddy told me to say". I said to the young lad, "Go downstairs and tell your daddy I want to see him". The little old man came up and started his story in the usual manner. I said: "Look, pop, this has been going on for three years. I have run out of reasons for visiting you. Either you must trust me or say that you do not, in which case we will go no further". I said that I could not accept the story he had told me and knew that it was not the truth. I outlined to the old man what I felt was the true story. He said, "You are pretty near right, Mr. More. I will tell you this." When he had finished his story I felt that I finally had some idea of the truth. I gave him advice about further action. That was a Saturday and on the following Monday he went to the immigration office. Within two months he was regularized. Today he has made an application for his family to come to Canada. I hope his family will be able to come within a short period of time.
Mr. Chairman, the facts I have just related apply to a family of which I have some knowledge. These people should be given the understanding that their status can be regularized if they will tell the truth. Each year these people are learning to trust their friends and believe in the assurances because of satisfactory treatment other individuals have received. They are beginning to believe that they will not receive discriminatory treatment. There are many hundreds of people who I believe will come forward soon and tell the true facts. The program in question has really only been operating effectively for two years rather than four. Someone has worked very hard over a period of two years in an attempt to break down the fear these unfortunate people have. I refer again to what the hon.

not think the gates should be closed at the end of this month. The program should continue for at least 12 months. The least I ask of the minister at this time is that he give notice here and now that the doors are open and that the program is available. Give it publicly and make it widely known. I will certainly make it known to the people of my community that the program will be finished by the first of September or the end of September, 1965. Having undertaken a humane program which was brought about as a result of discrimination throughout the history of the Chinese in Canada, please do not eliminate completely the benefit of that program by only two weeks warning that the program is finished.
There is discrimination in the act and nothing can cover it up. I concur fully in the remarks of the hon. member for Greenwood in this regard. It is something of which no Canadian can be proud. As I say, we know that the older Chinese have not assimilated but have carried on their old Chinese ways. On the other hand, their sons and daughters are the equal of any in school and the equal of any of us as citizens of Canada. I ask the minister to consider these points well. I thank him for his co-operation and personal consideration whenever it has been necessary to approach him.

I was disappointed that the minister did not make a statement on a matter that has been very close to me as chairman of the immigration committee of the Anglican church. For 14 months I have waited at the minister's door at various times and the doors of other officials with regard to a program that seemed to me to have wide acceptance within the department. I refer to the program under which church people would sponsor 50 boys from Hong Kong to come into this country for training and then to find their places as citizens.
I have been patient about this matter for 14 months. On many occasions during the question period and at other times when I
have wished to press the minister about it he has assured me that he would make a statement on this aspect of immigration. I think it is a rather humanitarian project although I admit that the numbers involved are just a drop in the bucket. However, he assured me that if I would wait until his estimates were presented I would have my answer. I followed his remarks about Hong Kong today with close attention and I should like to have the assurance that the department will accept the proposal of the Anglican Church of Canada and allow these boys to come to Canada under sponsorship to attend technical or other schools within the country. The minister having put me off, if I may use that term, for 14 months, I would be gravely disappointed if, after I and others who are interested in this project have waited so patiently, we were told that this program, which as I say has met with wide acceptance on the part of those officials of the department with whom I have spoken, was not going to be part of the over-all program. I would hope that within the next few minutes the minister would give me a favourable answer in this regard.
I want to say how much I appreciated the remarks of the hon. member for St. Paul's and the hon. member for Greenwood. I think that immigration is not a partisan matter, in the sense that problems concerning immigration and the provisions of the Immigration Act are brought forward by members in all parts of the house. But I must say I agree with the hon. member for Greenwood in his reference to the really splendid statement about amending the act. If I ever heard something written in an office to be uttered through the mouth of the minister, it was this statement. I want to repeat it because I suppose the same thing has been said by every minister whenever he has not wanted to make a move, and I have to admit that people have tried to put such things into my mouth at times. These are his words:
There are many inter-relationships between various sections of the act and isolated amendments, while perhaps appropriate in respect of one or more particular problems, could have unfortunate effects in other areas.
This has been said a thousand times before in the house and it is not good enough. For the life of me I cannot understand this worship at the altar of the sanctity of a statute. If we did our job properly in this place we would have two or three amendments to the act a year, provided they were sensible ones and commended themselves to the majority of members. But, no, the act is some sacred
6852	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration thing on an altar; we all come to bow down and genuflect before the act. I believe that answer is not good enough. If there are amendments suggested by the courts or by members, then for heaven's sake they should be made. Then, in the years to come we could have a consolidation of the act. Then, we could have it revised and revised again to look after all the small problems. This sanctity of the statute is nothing more than nonsense in my opinion.
Having said that, I hope there will be a committee of the house on immigration soon. There is a wide interest amongst the members in such a committee. We would like to hear about the plans the minister has. We commend him for them. The hon. member for Regina City complimented the minister and his parliamentary secretary. I should like to add my compliments. I should like also to compliment the new deputy minister. I see that Maclean's magazine classifies him as a submandarin, whatever that is. He has been a wonderful addition to the department and I thank him for the courtesy he has shown to me. I hope he did not have anything to do with the writing of this nonsensical sentence about the sanctity of the statute, because it is nothing more than nonsense.

Mr. Chairman, the members of my constituency were very pleased with the speech made by the minister in this house on August 4. What they found to be very encouraging was the statement made which appears on page 6394 of Hansard, to this effect:
As far as Immigration is concerned, I have already stated in the house that we have now reached a point where a positive and aggressive policy in immigration matters should be established in our country.
Then on the next page I find this statement:
Later, when the business of the house will permit, I hope to make a revision of the Immigration Act, so that it may be more in keeping with the requirements of the twentieth century and the situation in which find themselves modem states which need more and more to welcome new citizens who are willing to go there.
Perhaps with respect to the question of the twentieth century we might be at the stage in our history at which the United States was in the nineteenth century. Perhaps we ought to borrow some of the aspects of the immigration policy of the United States in the nineteenth century when we are speaking about immigration into Canada in the twentieth century. This speech received unanimous editorial support in the country. I
[Mr. Fairweather.J

should like to refer to an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen yesterday which stated, amongst other things, the following:
That must be quite an immigration policy that immigration minister Tremblay and his colleagues are hammering out. Mr. Tremblay has been promising a new approach to the whole question of immigration, particularly with respect to regulations governing the entry of newcomers from Asian and Middle East countries, ever since he assumed his present portfolio in January.
Then, it says further:
Just over 93,000 immigrants came to Canada in 1963-a pitiable low figure for a country of Canada's size and natural resources.
Now, I should like to point out to the minister that if you take the train from Montreal and you travel east to the maritime provinces you can travel hundreds of miles without seeing a house. If you take a train from the city of Toronto and you travel west to Winnipeg you also travel hundreds of miles without seeing a house. We must ask ourselves if we are being moral in this country when we have over 3.5 million square miles of territory with only 19 million people in it. I am serious when I say that we must question ourselves also when we condemn the policy of apartheid in South Africa as to whether or not perhaps we are practising a passive form of apartheid in Canada by refusing to admit people to this country. What is the use of condemning South Africa if we will do nothing about the British West Indies?
In the Montreal Gazette of this morning the editorial states:
Immigration has fallen so low that probably almost as many Canadians are leaving the country as are coming in. The curtailment of immigration from its high point of 282,164 in 1957 was at first deliberate Canadian policy, the outcome of the slowdown in the economy. But there has been no slowdown the past few years. And yet the flow of immigration has not recovered.
The hard truth is that people no longer want to come to Canada in the numbers they once did.
In this respect, I should like to say the following: At the end of world war II Canada was the fourth largest manufacturing country in the world. We were sending our products to the different markets in Europe. Now the markets to which we have been sending our products are manufacturing the products we used to send. I say that if we can no longer export the products, let us import the customers. When we speak of landed immigrants in this country, we should change the phraseology. When we speak of the 90,000 immigrants who came to this country as landed immigrants, we should speak of them as landed consumers.

The editorial in the Gazette goes on to say:
It has become clear now that the methods of the Canadian immigration department will have to be revolutionized. This does not mean that the standards set for immigrants will have to be lowered. But it does mean that Canada can no longer wait for prospective immigrants to put in their applications. Canada will have to go out after suitable immigrants.
In this respect there are, as the minister will confirm, thousands of applications waiting to be processed in Greece; thousands of applications waiting to be processed in Italy. We need more staff in these different countries in order to process these applications. May I say that in my constituency there are thousands upon thousands of Greek people who are ready to suffer all kinds of personal deprivation in order to bring their fathers, mothers, sisters and brothers from Greece or from Italy and the different countries in Europe.
Now, Mr. Chairman, recently there have been speeches made in the house with regard to the C.B.C. I am only mentioning this because the cost of the C.B.C. has been criticized. It is criticized because we are televising and broadcasting to too few people in this country. If we had double or treble the population we have we would still only require the kind of broadcasting and televising facilities that we have now.
We have two transcontinental railways in this country, one of which is costing the country millions of dollars every year simply because there are not enough people to make use of these railroads. We are also faced with the situation where we want to implement the recommendations of the Hall royal commission. A headline in yesterday's Gazette said this: "Plan for health package could raise taxes 50 per cent." If we had more people in this country such plans could operate economically.
The trouble is that we have not enough people in this country and with too few people we will never be a great nation. If we want to make this a great nation what we need is people to make it great. If there are people in this country who are concerned -and I am not-about the great colossus to the south, I ask how can we ever be in a position to do anything about that situation unless we are ready to admit people to this country? You cannot live beside a nation of 200 million people, with only 19 million here, and be expected to be able to compete with it in any way, shape or form.
We have every natural resource in this country except one, people. That is the one 20220-434
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration natural resource we lack. So, Mr. Chairman, I hope that the policies yet to be enunciated by the minister will take into account some of the things that have been said here today. Canada should stop thinking in terms of what Canada can do for immigrants but should think in terms of what the immigrants can do for Canada.

I suppose I should join with other hon. members who have congratulated the minister on the excellence of his speech, but if I do not, Mr. Chairman, it is not because I have anything specifically against the minister or his speech. It is simply because I have heard other ministers make the same kind of speech. The former minister made a wonderful speech last year. Ministers in earlier governments, both Liberal and Conservative, all made the same kind of speeches. I suppose they came out of the same file, because if one does not do anything to implement the speech that was made the previous year, there is not much point in writing a new speech.
Not for a moment do I believe that the method which the minister announced today, to increase the number of immigrants coming to Canada, will be any more successful than were the methods announced by the former minister. Let us face cold hard facts. The people who have come to Canada ever since those of us who are not Indians started coming here and the type of people we have wanted to encourage, were those who came from northern and western Europe. In recent years those people have virtually stopped coming.
The minister is making a big mistake if he believes that by opening more immigration offices he will attract more people from Great Britain, Norway, Sweden, Holland, Belgium or Germany. The peoples of those countries are pretty intelligent and well informed. That is why we want them here, but that is also why they will not come here. Why should they come from those countries when they have full employment at home, and have had it for the last half dozen or more years, and when they know we have had large scale unemployment for the last 10 years? Even though the unemployment figures are down somewhat, there is no prospect that this coming winter we will not again have somewhere in the neighbourhood of 500,000 unemployed.
Similarly, persons who have families in those countries will look at the kind of medicare plans presently operating in those countries, financed to a large extent if not en-
6854	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration tirely by their governments. If they do this they will not come to Canada because the pension plans they enjoy at present fall far short of the pension schemes we have in Canada, indeed far short of the projected Canada pension plan which is to begin in a year or so but which will take at least 10 years to become fully operative. If we are going to have large scale immigration from Europe it will have to be from the countries of southern Europe.
I do not intend to speak for long about the kind of treatment meted out to people who have come to this country somewhat illegally. On another occasion the hon. member for Royal said this was the kind of person we wanted, the kind of person who has the gumption to jump ship and break the laws. These people have been put in jail for 30, 60 or a hundred days before their trials, at which they have been sentenced to two, three or five months in prison and then deported. Certainly they will not spread any encouragement to people in their home countries to come to Canada.
It is time for the department to take a hard look at the situation behind the iron curtain. Many people who entered Canada since world war II originally came from countries which are now behind the iron curtain. They were displaced during the war. They were in concentration camps or slave labour camps. They were working in factories in France, where they had been transported by the occupying armies of nazi Germany, and after the war they found their way to Canada. I join with members who have already spoken in saying this was a good thing for Canada and that we are happy to have them here.
Many of these people were separated from their families, some from wives, some from children, some from cousins, nephews or nieces. Like many other hon. members I too represent a constituency populated by a large number of people who came to Canada from Europe following world war II, and who have relatives living in countries behind the iron curtain. I know of cases, as I am sure do other hon. members, of people who are already citizens here and who have cousins, nephews, sons-in-law and other relatives in countries such as Hungary, Rumania, Yugoslavia and Poland. It seems to me we all should practise some of the compassion we are so glad to prate about. I understand the need for security regulations and I am not too critical of them, but it seems to me if we are to encourage the relatives of those people


who are already here to come to Canada we must be more elastic in our interpretation of them than we have been in the past. I hope the minister will take a sympathetic look at this matter. I know he can say with justification that he has been co-operative, as was his predecessor, with regard to individual cases. I have been successful in some of these cases. I know the hon. member for Toronto Greenwood has been successful. My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre says he has been successful. I, personally, do not take any credit when I am successful in one of these cases because I think that if a person has to go to his member of parliament in a case of this sort, then, rather than being proud that I have succeeded I feel I ought to be ashamed that the regulations are such as to make it necessary for anyone to take that course. I think the regulations should be such that a person could get permission to enter Canada simply by going to the local office of the department of immigration and making an application. I am not saying we should open the doors wide. I am not saying that if some member of a central committee of the communist party or some minister in the communist government of one of the countries behind the iron curtain wanted to come to Canada we should say: Come on in, we are making it easy. All I am asking is that the tens of thousands of people who are living here and who have relatives who wish to come to Canada should be given a great deal of encouragement.
I should like to say something, now, about what I consider to be the total inadequacy of the change in the regulations which the minister intends to make with respect to this act. I will not repeat the exact words he used. A previous speaker has already done that. When they are read aloud it becomes apparent how ludicrous the concession is. Nor am I satisfied with the minister's promise that he is looking into this question and that we shall soon be getting a complete revision of the act. This is what the former minister of citizenship and immigration said last year. Ministers have been saying it for a long time.
I have before me a memorandum presented to the government of Canada by the Canadian Labour Congress dated March 14, 1962. So it was presented to the former government. This memorandum says, with regard to some changes which were proposed by the minister of citizenship and immigration at that time:
While gratified with what appear to be changes for the better, we are bound to express dis-

appointment that the Immigration Act itself has remained unchanged. There has been widespread agreement, including expressions from your government, that the act should be overhauled, and the congress among others had anticipated an amended act rather than only a change in the regulations. We urge immediate consideration of amendments to an act which has proved obviously unsatisfactory in many respects.
I wonder for how many more sessions and how many more years members on all sides of the house will have to get up and make statements of that kind. I do not believe that this minister or any other minister ever came into the house and told a deliberate lie. What is the sacred cow which prohibits every minister, despite the fact that he sets out with the best of intentions, from bringing about this revision? Every minister has made the same kind of statement: We are getting to it; it won't be long. I do not wish to heap coals of fire, but I hope it will not be as long as it has taken the Liberal party to bring in a pension plan, that is, 35 or 40 years. Surely it is time, now, that the Immigration Act was completely revised along lines which have been indicated so often and so eloquently by spokesmen from all parties in years gone by.
I should like to say something about the discriminatory features which still exist in the act and the regulations. I am constantly amazed at the way in which ministers can make speeches expressing sentiments of equality and justice which are so obviously false. I do not know whether the minister just blinds himself-
