speechtext: Shame.

The minister of health says "shame". Let me give a couple of examples. There is not a minister with whom I have had a better or more successful relationship than the present Minister of Justice. On September 23, 1963, that hon. gentleman made a speech to the Chinese community in Vancouver during which he said:
I have been distressed by the accusations of discrimination which have reached me. If prejudice exists in immigration matters it must be eliminated. True Canadianism permits no discrimination. All citizens are equal in rights and responsibilities, regardless of ethnic origin or creed. It is with this view in mind that I am most sincere in my efforts to weed out discrimination and prejudice.
That is a wonderful statement. But today his colleague announces that in two weeks time the amnesty program for the benefit of Chinese who are here illegally will be discontinued. I would point out that this is a program which has only just started to pro-20220-4341
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration duce results. I would remind the minister of health that the only group which will be affected, the group for whom this program was adopted consists of the Chinese, and I suggest that when the former minister of citizenship and immigration made that speech to the Chinese community he must have been speaking with his tongue in his cheek.
During the last session, the hon. member for Greenwood raised the question of a Canadian-born citizen of Chinese origin, Wayson Choy who had applied to be allowed to enter the United States and who was turned down because of his Chinese origin despite the fact that, like most of us in this house, he had been born in Canada. The Prime Minister made the following statement on October 28:
At the outset I should like to make it very clear that as for Canadian law and policy the present government, like its predecessor, is firmly opposed in principle and in practice to racial discrimination.
That sounds very good. But anyone who looks at the Immigration Act and its regulations will readily see how ludicrous statements of this kind are.
I am sorry I do not have my files with me this afternoon-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: He does not need them.

I have to smile at the cheers from those on the benches to my right. Having sat here day in and day out, listening for many hours to the drivel which comes from some of those members I admit I have to smile at their hope that we will co-operate to get on with our business. Suddenly they become great believers in speed and efficiency in this parliament.
The regulations which we have today are designed to a large extent to keep out of Canada those people whose colour is not white. If hon. members opposite do not believe me, if the minister does not believe this is true, I would point out that the people he has to convince are not, those of us who sit on this side of the chamber; he has to convince not only the Chinese of Hong Kong but he has to convince and educate the vast majority of British subjects, citizens of the commonwealth, who live in the West Indies.
As I was going to say before I was so rudely interrupted, in the last year we have had visits to Canada from the prime ministers of some of the West Indian countries. I am speaking from memory, Mr. Chairman, but it seems to me the prime minister of Barbados was here, the prime minister of Trinidad, the
6856	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration prime minister of Tobago, and I think the prime minister of the Windward Islands. All of them mentioned the same fact, that their people find it virtually impossible to come to Canada. The proof is very simple to find, if one wants to look for it, if one wants to be realistic instead of having one's head in the clouds like the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
Just consider the tens of thousands, the hundreds of thousands of people who have gone from Jamaica, from Trinidad and from Barbados to the British Isles; so much so that they have had their difficulties there. But why have they gone to Great Britain rather than Canada? They have done this because the British, very reasonably, have done nothing to keep them out; while we, on the contrary, have done a great deal to keep them out. I and other hon. members who handle immigration cases have had the same experience. There have been many cases of West Indians, people from Jamaica, Trinidad and the other countries of the West Indies who have come to Canada to study, who have spent a year, or two or three years getting the kind of training which every minister has said develops the kind of person we want in this country, they have become skilled in some craft, and yet when they decide to stay in Canada, on the basis of their experience here, having had the kind of training they have had, they have found it virtually impossible to get the minister or the department to permit them to stay. So I say that if the minister wants to make his speeches mean something, if he wants to be honest, he ought to consider what happens to those people from the West Indies and he ought to clean up the mess that still exists.
Mr. Chairman, I now wish to deal briefly with some of the provisions of the Immigration Act. I hoped these provisions would have disappeared by now, as they would have if the minister had followed the speeches made by the former minister and had brought in a revised act, as he should have done. I would like to show just what these provisions do and how ridiculous was the statement made by the Prime Minister during the last session, in the light of the actual practices in Canada. Section 61 of the Immigration Act, in dealing with the regulations provides, by paragraph (g), that the governor in council may make regulations for the prohibiting or limiting of the admission of persons by reason of;
(i)	nationality, citizenship, ethnic group, occupation, class or geographical area of origin,
(ii)	peculiar customs, habits, modes of life or methods of holding property.


It might be interesting to find out some day just what the department considers to be "peculiar customs", because what is one person's peculiar customs may be somebody else's normal customs. Then paragraph (iii) says:
(iii)	unsuitability having regard to the climatic, economic, social, industrial, educational, labour, health or other conditions or requirements existing, temporarily or otherwise, in Canada or in the area or country from or through which such persons come to Canada, or
(iv)	probable inability to become readily assimilated or to assume the duties and responsibilities of Canadian citizenship within a reasonable time after their admission.
The regulations, which are the main means of controlling immigration to Canada, still contain provisions which in effect, if not in language, discriminate on geographic, and hence racial grounds, in precisely the same way as the immigration laws of the United States, which were objected to by the Prime Minister so eloquently during the last session. The main section relating to admission to this country is regulation 31 of the immigration regulations passed on June 18, 1962. The former minister of citizenship and immigration was wont to repeat that these regulations would eliminate discrimination to some extent. We have succeeded in persuading the public of this, but in fact this discrimination still exists. The hon. member for Greenwood pointed out how regulation 36 classifies people. I quote from regulation 31 (d), which says that a person who is a citizen of any country of Europe, including Turkey, or of any country of North, Central or South America or islands adjacent thereto, or of Egypt, Israel or Lebanon is admitted if applied for by relatives in Canada on a fairly wide group of relationships, if such person is able and willing to provide care and maintenance.
I would point out that two very large and important members of the commonwealth, namely India and Pakistan, are among those countries which do not qualify under this regulation; so that citizens of India and Pakistan, as far as this country is concerned, as expressed in this regulation, are in fact second class citizens as compared with the citizens of other commonwealth countries. I am glad I am not one of those who go to commonwealth conferences representing this country, because I for one certainly could not justify this kind of discrimination, whatever the original reasons may have been.
I suggest to the minister that the time has long since passed when the house should be

put off with tinkering with the act and tinkering with the regulations. I know the minister is a new minister, but these matters must be known to the top officials of the department. I have a good deal of confidence in them, despite what some other hon. members, or one member, may think; I have confidence that they must have done a great deal of work along the lines which have already been discussed so often in this house. I suggest that the minister should get busy and correct these matters by a very early date. I suppose it is too late to hope that during this session or during 1964 we will have an amended Immigration Act. I should like to say to the minister that this session will last some time yet. We have a lot of business that must be done, and I am not convinced that he believes an amendment to the Immigration Act is high on the priority list and will be brought forward this year. I do state, however, that if we consider his estimates in 1965 and there has not been a new act brought forward he will have a long, rough, hard, bumpy time before they pass.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to deal with one or two other matters, and will do so briefly at this time. I do not intend to go into detail in referring to the debates that have already taken place during this session in respect of the kind of treatment meted out to people who have come into Canada illegally. The minister made an excellent statement about this matter. The minister has appointed eminent counsel to investigate the situation. I know Mr. Sedgwick is now working on this task and I do not raise this subject as a result of any prejudgment to the effect that Mr. Sedgwick will not present a good report. Surely the department will have to wait until it receives Mr. Sedgwick's report before eliminating some of the horrible practices which in my mind have existed and still exist. The minister can give a detailed explanation to the best of his ability in respect of each case, but in my opinion he cannot in any way justify the fact that a number of people have been kept in prisons for 30, 60, 90 or 100 days before their cases have been settled. The minister cannot in any way justify the fact that a large percentage of those people were brought before magistrates, tried, convicted, sentenced and jailed, although not represented by counsel.
I have said before that I do not believe any person should be tried for an offence for which he can be jailed upon conviction without the benefit of counsel. Certainly no individual in Canada illegally, without friends,
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration contacts and probably no money, should be subjected to that kind of treatment. The department should make arrangements to provide counsel for these individuals. These arrangements would necessitate the spending of a good deal of money, but I feel it would be money well spent. This country would have the kind of reputation for fairness and decency we think we are entitled to as a result of following that suggested practice.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make one further remark in respect of individuals being kept in jail while their cases are being investigated. I am not at all satisfied with the arrangements made by the department. In Toronto and Montreal these people are being held in Don and Bordeaux jails while their cases are being investigated. I placed a question about this situation on the order paper several weeks ago, and that question has not been answered. My understanding is that these people who are still being held in those jails because they are here illegally, are subject to the same rules and regulations as apply to other inmates.

speechtext: Order. I must interrupt the hon. gentleman. His time has expired.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether I may be allowed to speak for one minute to complete my remarks in respect of this subject?
Agreed.

I feel that the department is responsible for these people being kept in these jails. The department made the arrangements to do this. I am told that visitors of the people being held in the Bordeaux jail can only visit once or twice each week, that mail privileges are very restricted and that visitors are being fingerprinted. Surely Mr. Chairman, if a large number of people are to be held, pending investigation of their cases, the department should make arrangements to keep these people at some place other than the local jail.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to limit the debate on immigration. It is the duty of each member who desires to comment on immigration estimates following my statement, to do so. However, before commenting on the remarks made by hon. gentlemen I should like to make a statement about Indian affairs.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is it the wish of the committee at this stage to hear the minister's statement on Indian affairs? There may be
6858	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration other members who wish to speak on immigration matters. Is it agreed that the minister make a statement at this time?
I do not wish to limit the debate.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to speak very briefly about immigration matters. Perhaps if I am allowed three minutes I can assist in facilitating the conclusion of the discussion on immigration. Certainly we have no intention of extending the discussion this afternoon, and we felt that there was ample time to discuss the estimates of this department when we were considering interim supply. Because of that fact, it is our hope we will be able to conclude our consideration of the estimates of this department this afternoon.
Several individuals, including the minister, have referred to a new age and spirit about to emerge in regard to Canada's attitude towards immigration. That was the theme of the minister's statement. He referred to the developments that are to take place in the future. The hon. member who just spoke referred to the necessity for a new approach to immigration, and I should like to point out to him and other hon. members that a change in regulations was made in 1962 which provided a new approach to immigration matters. All that is needed to achieve a broader perspective is the application of a more enlightened spirit and policy in the administrative approach.
The main problem that did exist under the old discriminatory approach to immigration was the limiting of unsponsored categories to rather exclusive groups. When the new regulations are applied, in the spirit in which they should be applied, there will be absolutely no limitation to unsponsored immigrants. Immigrants may come to Canada from any place in the world, provided they have the educational background and skills to make it possible for them to fit into Canada's economy.
Are you referring to the changes made in 1962?

I was referring to the changes brought forward by the former government in 1962 and approved by this parliament.
The refugee category was also broadened at that time. This category was restricted to refugees from Europe until 1962, at which time it was changed, making it possible to meet special emergency circumstances. The refugee provisions now apply to any group
[The Chairman.]

anywhere in the world. I think we have demonstrated a means of meeting some of the problems that have been referred to by various members during this discussion this afternoon. These problems can be solved by broadening our approach to the problem. The minister has indicated that new administrative techniques are going to be applied. Certainly the regulations that were passed in 1962 depend upon the broadening of the administrative facilities and there are two questions I should like to ask in regard to office facilities. I refer first to the West Indies. Up until a few years ago there was no permanent headquarters in the West Indies and immigration was taken care of by a mobile immigration team. I think this gave rise to the problems that were outlined by the hon. member for Winnipeg North. Certainly here is a country where many people are interested in coming to Canada. The regulations now make it possible for them to come to Canada if the administrative means are provided in order to make it possible.
I should also like to ask the minister about the administrative facilities available in Greece where there seems to have been some sort of bottleneck in the past. I feel that the regulations of 1962 are adequate to meet most, if not all, of the problems that have been raised in the discussion this afternoon.

Mr. Chairman, I propose to take only a few minutes of the time of the committee to make some comments about the operations of the department with respect to immigration. I might say in passing that I was interested to note the words of one of the members of the opposition with regard to the deputy minister being referred to in a Canadian magazine as a member of the mandarin class. This may be an omen of hope to those in the house who are interested in increasing Chinese immigration. I do not really know, but I know that we wish him well in his attempt to carry out some positive changes in the department.
In any event, Mr. Chairman, I was pleased to note the positive steps that were mentioned in the minister's statement, particularly those dealing with increasing the staffs in overseas offices, putting them in proper quarters, and general changes and improvements in administrative practices. However, I say, I hope in a constructive spirit and with the utmost respect, that statements and speeches favouring a positive approach to immigration and even the broadening of the regulations themselves will not mean too much unless there are at the same time the staff and the administrative

machinery needed to handle the admission of sizeable numbers of immigrants in a prompt and courteous manner, and even more important is the need for an attitude in the department from top to bottom that this department is a department of immigration and that immigrants are needed and useful to this country.
The lack of effect of changes in the regulations unless backed up by proper administrative machinery and proper attitudes is shown by the record of the previous Conservative government. I was interested to hear the comments of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris on this point. In the years between 1945 and 1957 I must say that under the regulations which then existed and which have been criticized by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris and other members, over
1.600.000	immigrants came to Canada, all of them under a Liberal administration, and the overwhelming majority of them became good, useful and productive citizens. In 1956 the last full year of Liberal government 164,857 people came to this country and in 1957 the number rose to 282,164. In 1958, the first full year of Conservative government, the number dropped to 124,851 and it dropped each year thereafter until in 1961 it fell to a shameful low of 71,684. I might say that if the excuse is given that economic conditions had deteriorated at that time I think members of the opposition are caught in a difficult dilemma because I had understood their comments in this house to be that in those years there were no economic difficulties, and in fact in 1961 improvement had begun.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

I will accept questions at the end of my remarks, which will not be too prolonged if the hon. member does not mind. In January, 1962 the new regulations referred to by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris were proclaimed. What happened then? Was there a dramatic increase in immigration? No. The number increased by less than
3.000	to 74,586. Therefore the changed regulations apparently meant very little under the previous administration since there appeared to be a failure to fill staff vacancies and perhaps there was even an actual decrease in staff. I think it can be said that the attitude of the previous government was exemplified by the minister of that time, Mrs. Fairclough, who on behalf of the government was responsible for a very unfortunate order in council limiting Italian immigration. In any
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration event, since the present administration took office there at least has been a start toward improvement, with immigration rising in 1963 to some 93,000.
But, Mr. Chairman, this is only a start toward improvement. There is a lot more that can and must be done, and much of it need not wait for changes in legislation because the vast powers given to the minister and the government under the present act to deal with these matters through order in council, thereby changing the regulations, are such that changes can have a far reaching effect if put into effect in this way. These changes in departmental organization and administrative practice can have a far reaching and useful effect.
I might say to those who are particularly interested, as I am, in having changes made in the legislation, which can only be done through being introduced in the house, that if members of the official opposition would be kind enough to permit the resolution and amendments now pending before the house to come to a vote it would be a lot easier to have other needed legislation, including changes in the Immigration Act, brought before us for implementation, and it could be done a lot quicker.
I noted the minister's reference in his statement to the link between the number of immigrants to be admitted and the administrative apparatus of the department. But, Mr. Chairman, our aim should not be to hold back the number of immigrants to fit the administrative apparatus of the department. Instead our aim should be to expand the administrative apparatus of the department to meet the needs of this country for an expanded population through immigration.
It is important to look for people abroad with high degrees of skill and training, but there is still room in this country for people who bring with them not much more than basic intelligence, good health and the desire to make a contribution to our country's life. If we expect suddenly to get very large numbers of immigrants from Europe, for example, with very high degrees of skill, education and training, I think that to a certain extent we are fooling ourselves. It is true, however, that through better promotion and more staff abroad we can get more immigrants of this type. With the dramatically improved economic conditions in western Europe and the opportunities there the high proportion of skilled people who might have wanted to
6860	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration come here 10 years ago is no longer available.
I hope that this emphasis on skill and training will not be used by the department officials as a subtle way to keep people out. It is true that we must try to match the flow and type of immigration to the type of skills needed, the type of jobs available and the economic conditions of the country, but we are not going to have tens of thousands of Ph.D.'s in atomic physics, or computer technicians battering at our doors to get into Canada. If we want to expand the population of the country more quickly than natural increase will permit and in some way to balance the outflow to other countries, we are going to have to make it possible for substantial numbers of people to come here who have relatively low degrees of formal skills and training when they arrive.
There is no question but that an expanded population increases jobs for all and helps the economy to grow. One basic answer to our economic problems is a larger population. This is shown by the fact that the United States, with the same type of geographic divisions and difficulties, has a population of some 190 million providing a huge internal market so that that country is not exposed in the same way as our own to external economic changes.
Just by way of conclusion, Mr. Chairman, let me suggest that my own community of Windsor is a wonderful example of how people coming from almost every part of the world, the British Isles, western Europe, central and eastern Europe, the Mediterranean countries and the Orient, can work and live together in harmony and make a great and positive contribution to this country.
There is still a lot more to be done toward making the law more just and equitable, toward making more effective and generally improving both the act and the regulations as well as the operations of the department itself. I say by way of conclusion that the record of the previous Liberal government between 1945 and 1957 in bringing almost two million immigrants to this country, while at the same time giving us an expanding economy with expanding employment opportunities for all, is an indication of the achievement that can come, and I am confident will come, in the very near future.

May I be allowed just a brief question of the hon. member? I wonder if he is aware that one of the major reasons for changing the regulations in 1962 was that


the traditional source of immigrants was drying up in Europe as a result of the economic boom, and instead of sending people abroad, countries such as Germany and France were inviting immigrants to meet their employment needs? This was the reason for broadening on such an extensive basis the categories of immigrants. Is he aware also, as the minister outlined today, that as the result of the regulation changes there was a dramatic upsurge in immigrants coming in from Hong Kong, for example, in 1962 and 1963?
Then, there is the joint provincial responsibility in immigration matters. I am sure he is aware of the dynamic immigration program that was sponsored by the Ontario government in the immediate post-war years, which was one of the most successful immigration schemes.

If I may reply briefly to my hon. friend's very interesting question, I should like to direct his attention to an interesting editorial in the Globe and Mail for June 10, 1964, entitled "A Tale of Two Countries". This editorial points out that at a time when our immigration was decreasing in a drastic manner, some one million immigrants from Italy, Greece, Portugal and Spain went to West Germany and 100,000 more are expected to go there this year. As the editorial points out so well:
In these figures and facts there are two morals for Canada. One is that a lively, competitive economy can absorb almost any amount of immigration.
Then, I quote from the editorial again:
The other moral Canada may draw from the West German story is that there is still a substantial pool of ambitious manpower and woman-power in southern Europe. If West Germany can get large numbers of these people to settle there temporarily, cannot we get large numbers of them to settle here permanently?
I have, in my reply, only to echo these statements and point out that if last year we only got 14,427 people from Italy and 4,759 from Greece it shows that even under the regulations to which my hon. friend refers, there is still a lot more that Canada could and should do in this regard.

As regards Indian affairs, I would like to reiterate that my aim with regard to Indians is to help them participate fully in the social and economic life of this country. We are pursuing this aim through a wide range of programs aimed at the development of the individual and the development of the community. Throughout the em-

phasis is on the progressive involvement of the Indians in both planning and execution. Again, we are seeking to bring about the further extension to Indians of services normally available to other citizens. This will involve continuing consultation not only with the provinces and with other federal departments but with the Indians themselves for we know the importance of obtaining their views on matters which are of direct concern to them.
I want to review in some detail the current Indian affairs programs. However, before doing so, I would like to speak of three or four matters which also deserve attention and which are occupying much of my thought and energy at this time.
Hon. members will recall that the administration of Indian affairs was considered at the federal-provincial conference held in November, 1963. It was agreed by the delegates that the matter was so complex as to warrant a federal-provincial ministerial conference and plans are proceeding toward this end.
In the months that have intervened since November we have been developing various proposals aimed at encouraging greater provincial interest and co-operation in Indian affairs always with the basic objective of providing Indians with the same opportunities for social and economic advancement as are enjoyed by other citizens. We know that the provinces have also used the intervening period to good advantage in considering what part they might play in furthering the basic objectives agreed upon at the November conference.
We intend to keep the Indians fully informed with regard to the further extension of provincial services to them. I have already written to the council of each band explaining the exploratory purpose of the November conference and will keep them up to date as developments occur.
In keeping with our wish to consult the Indians on all matters of direct concern to them, the Indian claims Bill No. C-130, as introduced in the house on December 14 last, was sent in January to Indian bands, Indian organizations and others throughout the country. I am glad to say we have been having a generally good response to this with nearly 250 bands already heard from. Some 31 replies have been received from other sources. Close study will be given to the various suggestions made before proceeding with the legislation.

It would also be my hope that we can begin to move ahead over the next year with appropriate amendments to the Indian Act. Much of the ground work has been done already. On the other hand, it is not something we want to rush through without a great deal of careful thought. What is more, our legislative thinking must be reshaped to some extent by current and possibly quite new developments in the Indian affairs field, not the least of which are the promotion of closer co-operation with the provinces, and the community development approach of which I will be speaking later.
I have mentioned Indian consultation in connection with the possible further extension of normal federal and provincial services to Indians and in regard to the Indian claims bill. I would also confirm here what has been said before about the Indian Act, namely that this government would consult with the Indians on any proposed changes. Consultation is not, of course, an easy task when there are over 550 bands and a dozen or more Indian organizations. Much thought is being given to ways and means of providing for more ready access to Indian opinion at all levels-band, regional and national. I am confident we shall be able to work something out in this respect that will be satisfactory to the Indians and the government alike.
As well as through direct consultation with the Indians we hope to learn much from the Indian research project which was announced in the house on December 2 last and which is now in the field study stage. The research director, Dr. H. B. Hawthorn, has informed me that he and Dr. Adelard Tremblay, associate director, have been successful in gathering a very capable group to work on the project. As stated in December the purpose of the project is to provide a body of knowledge that will assist in establishing guidelines for future policy and the over-all planning required to promote the welfare and progress of Canadian Indians. I am sure that much valuable information will soon begin to flow from the study which is unique in Canadian experience.
Before going on to review the Indian affairs programs, I would like to mention that although I am greatly interested in the wellbeing of the Indians, matters relating directly to Indian health come within the jurisdiction of the Department of National Health and Welfare. I am of course, willing to take up with my colleague questions which may arise concerning Indian health. However, I would point out that hon. members will be given

Basic to the work of the Indian affairs branch is the education program. The estimates for 1964-65 reflect the continued emphasis on the program with 57.55 per cent of the amount requested designated for Indian education, including $27,200,000 for the administration, operation and maintenance of the school program, and $7,416,000 for capital expenditures. This represents an anticipated increased cost for education of $3,528,190 or 11.3 per cent over the previous year. Of this amount about 3 per cent is attributable to a higher enrolment in schools of all kinds, 2.8 per cent to rising costs including higher payments to provincial school boards, 1.7 per cent to an accelerated program of building repairs to maintain minimum standards of school accommodation, and 3.8 per cent for new construction.
School enrolment continues to increase at a steady pace with the school population for the 1963-64 academic year standing at 55,475 or an increase of approximately 5,000 over the previous year. The largest part of this increase was due to the admission of approximately 4,200 more pupils in provincial schools.
To facilitate the further enrolment of Indian pupils in the provincial school systems, provision has been made in the proposed capital expenditures for contributions towards provincial school facilities of approximately $2,345,000 as compared to expenditures for this purpose during 1963-64 of approximately $1,913,000. Payments to provincial schools for tuition fees for Indian pupils have also continued to increase proportionately, and expenditures of approximately $4,255,000 are anticipated, an increase of $465,000 over last year.
Our government has continued to provide financial assistance to worthy Indian students to enable them to follow academic, professional or vocational courses so long as the students display reasonable promise and industry. During the year 22 special scholarships were awarded to outstanding students for studies in engineering, nursing, medicine, teacher training, metallurgy, auto mechanics, diesel mechanics, carpentry, music and commercial art. In addition financial assistance according to need was given to over
4,000	pupils to enable them to attend high school or university, or to obtain professional training.


I am endeavouring to develop a basis for the establishment of school boards on reserves which would assume responsibility for the operation of reserve schools in accordance with provincial legislation and under the direction of provincial education administration. It is hoped that in the near future pilot projects of this nature will be conducted in selected areas.
The number of Indian students attending schools providing trades and professional training more than doubled during the past year. To accelerate the increase even more, it is intended to give added emphasis to this field of education in the coming year. In addition to the regular trade schools, the Indian affairs branch conducts special courses to provide vocational training in such activities as guiding and boat building.
The growing importance of economic development programs to many Indians in all walks of life is reflected in the estimates. These are essentially self-help programs and wherever possible financial assistance from appropriation is furnished on a repayable basis. Last year a total of $163,000 was repaid, most of which was for materials and supplies used in wildlife and fishery projects and for advances for agricultural, handicraft and employment placement purposes.
Expenditures from appropriation are augmented by loans from a revolving loan fund and by expenditures, grants, or loans from band trust funds. The revolving loan fund of $1,000,000, established as a source of credit for Indians who do not have access to ordinary lending institutions, is operating with about $750,000 out on loan at any time, leaving about one fourth of the fund available for new loans.
The use of band trust funds for economic development purposes is also increasing. Last year some $300,000 in band funds was diverted from direct relief to more constructive purposes including the improvement of reserve facilities. Seventy three projects were accepted by the Department of Labour for the winter works incentive program with an estimated 1,297 Indians employed for a total of over 20,000 man days. Payroll costs were $228,000 half of which is of course recoverable under the program.
Bands lacking sufficient funds to participate in the winter works incentive program are assisted under a special community employment program undertaken each year by the department. In the past year $1,200,000 was approved for this purpose. An additional sum of $414,000 was made available under the

federal supplementary government winter construction program to carry out works projects on reserves in 16 designated development areas.
Indians are encouraged to exploit and develop the natural assets of their reserves and the provision is made in the estimates for materials, supplies and equipment to help them in this. Programs of assistance to farmers and ranchers are being continued with the emphasis on livestock raising for which a promising rotating herd program has been established. The forest resources of Indian reserves are another important factor in their economy and harvesting by the Indians themselves has increased to 90 per cent as compared to 25 per cent 15 years ago. Oil and gas are providing Indian bands, mostly in Alberta, with an annual revenue of over $2 million.
There is a potential for industrial enterprise on many reserves that has been scarcely tapped. However, while development of this kind has so far been limited, this is an area where we hope that more can be done. To this end we have established a close working relationship with the Department of Industry and hope to take full advantage of their services. We will also need to considerably strengthen branch staff in this field.
The estimates reflect an expanded scale of activities to meet the demand for Indian handicrafts. More raw materials are being provided on a repayable basis while the need for broader distribution is being met through expansion of the department's central marketing facilities. My department recognizes that still greater attention needs to be given to this field and with this aim has recently taken on an arts and crafts development officer. This man will be examining the development of Indian handicraft to see in what way it can be further stimulated.
Development projects have been undertaken for the benefit of the very large group of Indians who still pursue their traditional vocations of hunting, fishing, trapping and wild crop harvesting. Since these projects are based on provincially-owned resources their success is dependent largely on continuation of the excellent co-operation now in effect either by formal cost-sharing agreements or informal work-sharing arrangements with the provinces concerned.
Assistance in commercial fishing is provided by supplying gear and in some cases freezing and storage facilities. Trappers are assisted by provision of grub stakes, essential supplies and equipment. In relation to both

Indians seeking wage employment are assisted through the department's employment placement program. Growing numbers of selected candidates are being placed in permanent employment in urban centres with the co-operation of the special services division of the national employment service. The total of such permanent placements in five years of operation has reached 2,124 of which 507 were placed in 1963-64. The majority of these were qualified for their jobs through academic and vocational training provided by the department.

Provision is again being made for a road construction program aimed at developing road systems on the more populated reserves and providing access to Indian groups who are living in isolation. Although progress has been made over the past several years in this field much remains to be done. It is hoped that further discussions with the provinces will result in better road facilities being made available to the Indians.

However, it is foreseen that much more will have to be done in future to keep pace with the steady increase in

Concern has been expressed about the apparent disparities between the amount of public assistance provided to Indians as compared to that received by other residents of the various provinces. On the surface there appear to be such disparities. However, they are more apparent than real. Indian assistance rates cover food only. Fuel, shelter, clothing and other forms of assistance are provided to Indians as extra items on the basis of need. On the other hand, provincial scales, though varying greatly from province to province, generally include a lump sum payment for food, shelter, clothing, fuel and other needs.
The problem in public assistance is not, therefore, one of amounts of assistance but rather that Indians receive assistance within one framework of administration while other citizens receive it within another. This tends to set Indians apart in a way which I think we all recognize as undesirable. So far the one exception is in Ontario where a number of bands participate under the provincial general welfare assistance act in the same way as other communities. It is the hope of the federal government that similar arrangements can eventually be made throughout the country.
Again, while arrangements have been made in some of the provinces for the extension of provincial and other child welfare services to Indians on reserves, I recognize the need for extending such services to all reserves as quickly as possible.
Despite the progress that is being made under existing programs it is recognized that additional positive measures of a preventive and remedial nature are needed to accelerate the process of bridging the social and economic gaps which are still all too common between Indians and non-Indians in this country. For some time this government has been giving close study to this problem and, as I announced in the house on July 7, has now developed a community development program to complement existing services in the fields of welfare, education, health and economic development and to assist in raising living standards and improving the economic, social and cultural life of the Indians.
This community development program will emphasize Indian participation and initiative in advancing the well-being of Indian communities and will result in the application of a community development approach in many


of the existing projects and services being provided by the Indian affairs branch.
As you were informed, it is expected that over the next three years this will involve an investment of over $3,500,000. The cost of this program is not included in these estimates but will be presented in supplementaries, at which time I will be prepared to answer any questions which hon. members may have.
This government is prepared to take the initiative in introducing a community development program on any Indian reserve which would benefit from this approach. Federal community development work would be phased into provincial operations whenever the Indians concerned are ready for this change and the province is able to extend itp own services. There will be no duplication of provincial services.
Although the community development program will affect in some ways the whole Indian affairs organization, a new social programs division is being created to reflect a new federal emphasis on the need to promote actively the development of Indian communities.
This new division will pull together and focus more effectively a number of services which have been provided in the past in a fragmentary way. This includes the current work being done in Indian leadership training and recreational services on Indian reserves.
The new social programs division will also include a "cultural affairs section" which will be staffed with Indians. This section will recognize the cultural needs of Indian communities and will facilitate the development of various forms of Indian cultural expression in the arts, including painting, sculpture, music, dancing and so on. Similar work will be done in the field of sports. Equal emphasis of course is being placed on the economic and social needs of Indian communities.
It will be necessary to appoint a number of community development officers to co-ordinate new and existing programs in the complex and demanding task of facilitating the development of Indian communities and giving them access to a wide range of technical and other resources which are available at the local, provincial and federal levels. Skilled practitioners in community development are extremely scarce in Canada, however. The federal government plans therefore to arrange additional training for appointees to equip them better for this work.

Training for community development officers constitutes only one aspect of the training that will be carried out. To accommodate the community development approach properly, Indian affairs branch will also be retraining its existing field staff.
Training courses are also being organized for Indians to fill jobs in the community development program. The aim is to create a group of trained and competent Indian employees as soon as possible to assist in the work of community development and eventually to fill positions of responsibility in Indian communities. In effect, Indian communities will be assisted to develop their own municipal type of civil service to manage welfare, recreational services, economic projects and many other local services.
Grants to Indian councils, particularly in communities in which such councils have achieved a measure of effectiveness will be an important instrument of development. Such assistance will supplement band revenues and is intended to make it possible for Indian councils to employ Indians full time in various community services.
The present adult education measures will be stepped up in the context of the community development program. Depending on the needs of various Indian communities, courses will be provided in such matters as budgeting, homemaking, food handling, sanitation and so on.
Within the framework of this program, there will be continuous consultation with Indian groups and individuals. Much of this consultation will take place informally and consideration is being given as well to a more formal structure of Indian advisory committees. These committees will be chosen by the Indian people and will be as broadly representative as possible.
In education, the influx of Indian pupils into provincial schools and training institutes has created a wide-spread need for adequate guidance services particularly for those students who are boarding in cities. Many students need much guidance and encouragement to make the necessary social adjustments to city life and city school study habits. The teacher-counsellor service provided by the branch must be strengthened each year to handle this problem. Indian age grade levels have been brought closer to provincial norms in recent years, but by reason of absenteeism and late starting there is still a relatively large number of children two or more years behind in their grades and who

Weights and Measures Act they commented on this bill which I am proposing. I just want to read a couple of paragraphs:
Two cartons of honey look just the same, but one holds 16 ounces and the other 12. Bottles of vinegar come at 8, 12, 16J, 24 and 33 ounces. Soap flakes of varying brands are in packages of 14 ounces, 16] ounces, 20 ounces, 20] ounces and 34 ounces. In these circumstances, the only way to figure out the best buy is with a sliderule, or maybe a computer. What is wrong with plain old pints and quarts, pounds and half-pounds? Could not the shopper's lot be made a bit easier? Or are the manufacturers deliberately trying to confuse her?
The purpose of my bill, Mr. Speaker, is to make it easier for the consumer. I hope that the government and the members of this house will facilitate the passage of the measure and give the government departments, both trade and commerce and health and welfare, as well as the new consumers advisory council, an opportunity to do their work as they should, without having their arms tied behind their backs.

Before the hon. member takes his seat, I wonder if I could ask him a question about his bill? Do I understand correctly that he is suggesting the administration should decide, in connection with cans of soup, for instance, that only cans of a certain size may be used by a manufacturer, and none other? Is that a correct interpretation?

That is correct. If the hon. member or the minister wish to have the details of what is involved in this bill they can get the evidence in the hearings that were held in the United States on the bill proposed by Senator Philip A. Hart of Michigan. Extensive and detailed hearings were held in which government and industry spokesmen gave full testimony. I believe all the information could be secured from this source.

We live
today in a society which is very largely dominated by advertising techniques and advertising philosophies. There is a story told of a man who said to his wife, "My dear, I have been made a vice president." She looked very sceptical and he said, "Are you not surprised?" She said, "Well, down at the groceteria there is a vice president in charge of prunes". He was incredulous, so he phoned the groceteria and said, "I want to speak to the vice president in charge of prunes". The girl said, "Yes, bulk or packaged?"
The advertisers, associated with the psychologists, in studying the mores of our society 

can almost predict our wants and can almost instruct us upon what we should buy. There is a story told by Vance Packard in his "The Hidden Persuaders" about a conversation between two psychologists. One of them said, "Now, take the man who drives a Studebaker, smokes Old Golds, uses cream-based hair oil, an electric shaver, carries a Parker 51 fountain pen. Obviously he's a salesman, an active man, aggressive in face to face situations and wants to make a good impression. Probably he was quite a romantic type in his youth". And the other psychologist added: "Also, you'll find that he is wearing loud shorts."
The psychologists, Mr. Speaker, allied with the merchandisers have developed a study of the techniques of impulse buying. As a matter of fact one psychologist who was studying merchandising techniques, realizing he could not give a lie detector test to the women who were shopping as to their reasons for choosing one product rather than another, decided to place a motion picture camera in a store to photograph the ladies as they went through the store. He counted the number of times her eyes blinked as an indication of how tense she was in making her merchandising decisions. The results were surprising to him. Instead of becoming more and more tense as she went through the store she became more and more relaxed. As a matter of fact, the blinking of her eyes decreased as she was going up and down the aisles to the extent that it became half of the normally expected rate.
A person can go into a store today and instead of facing the possibility of buying 600 items, he can choose between 6,000 and
8,000	items. The point made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) is a very salient comment about the merchandising habits of our society. I think that the individual salesman selling his wares can compare with the improved merchandising of, let us say, groceries. It has been discovered as the result of studies, that people going into a self-serve groceteria will buy a considerably larger number of items than people going into a grocery store in which they are served by a salesman. Impulse buying is that important. The person being sold by a salesman has time to weigh the pros and cons of a decision and may decide not to buy, whereas a person subject to impulse buying goes into a store in which the position of the item in the store, the colour of the package, the size of the package, the name of the item, are all decided on a scientific basis in order to induce the purchaser

to make his decision. When a person leaves the store he will have more items, it has been discovered, than he would have had if he had been served by a salesman. It has been discovered also that if there is any person more susceptible to impulse buying than the housewife, it is her husband. Men are even more subject to impulse buying than women.
As a result of these studies it has been decided that the size of the package, the colour of the package, the format, all these things are very important in terms of merchandising a product. The hon. member has introduced a bill concerning packaging. He mentioned the question of toothpaste in support of the point he made. I should like to read from the Consumers' Report of May, 1963 concerning one of the best known brands of toothpaste sold on this market. The report says that your correspondent's difficulty may be stated briefly as follows: One large tube, 1* ounces plus one family tube, ounces equals 6J ounces for 98 cents, as against two giant tubes, 2J ounces each equalling 5if ounces for 99 cents. The result is, Mr. Speaker, that the person buying the giant size tube of toothpaste is paying 22.61 cents per ounce while the person buying the family size tube pays 17.23 cents per ounce, a difference of more than 5 cents per ounce for the same brand of toothpaste, depending upon the size of the package.
Here is a form of what someone might call disguised taxation. Certainly there is a very wide differential between the merchandising packages. A very substantial levy is made on the people of Canada and the United States as well as other countries subject to this type of merchandising because of the packaging methods which are being used. Recently, in the field of cosmetics, the question of hollow wall packaging was examined by the attorney general of California. He accused 23 leading cosmetic companies of using deceptive packaging. It was found that by varying the package the customer was completely misled as to the amount of the product he was buying.
A very interesting study was made of aspirin in Baltimore city hospitals. Five different brands were examined and there was a report of the findings in the journal of the American medical association, December 29, 1962. I would like to quote from the report in Consumers' Report, where it says this:

Within days after the report appeared, the manufacturer of Bayer aspirin and the distributor of St. Joseph's aspirin began to capitalize on the fact that their products came out rather well in the study. Most upsetting to the federal trade commission and the American medical association was the advertising for Bayer aspirin which boasted that a "government-supported medical team," whose findings "were reported in the highly authoritative journal of the American medical association," had found the Bayer product equal to the higher-priced pain reliever. The ad further claimed that "Bayer aspirin brings relief that is as fast, as strong, and as gentle to the stomach as you can get. ...Bayer aspirin had a somewhat higher pain relief score than any of the other products."
In point of fact the study proved there was no difference in the pain relieving capabilities of the different brands, but that two brands, which contained phenacetin, tended to give more stomach upset.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to read a few extracts from a conference on consumer problems, sponsored by the Consumers' Association of Canada, to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) referred, in co-operation with the consumers union of the United States, held at Queen's University in 1962. I would like to read a comment made by Dr. C. A. Morrell, of the Department of National Health and Welfare, who said this:
Of the 2,263 people who said they wanted a change-
This is in packaging-
-1,061 wanted to change them because they thought packages were deceptive. This is nearly one in five people questioned and I think it is enough to give the packaging industry a reason for a critical review of what they are doing...
Although the possibility of deception is the main reason for Food and Drug to be interested in packaging, there are other reasons too. Packages should be of such construction and material that they cause no health hazards to the consumer. It is my feeling that some study should be made of vacuum sealed plastic packages to determine whether they should be used at all for packing certain kinds of meat and fish. Deaths from botulism derived from smoked fish sold in vacuum packed plastic containers occurred recently. Experimentally, at least, it has been possible to show the development of staphylococcus toxin in bacon, similarly packaged. The point to note is that under this kind of packaging the usual spoilage organisms did not develop and so the warning signs of bad odour and appearance were not there. Our own laboratory people said that had they not known the facts they would have had no objections to eating either the fish or bacon-they looked and smelled like good fish and bacon. New forms of packaging should not be introduced without careful forethought and study of possible hazards.

Certainly.

Does he think he could cure this evil by legislation or by competition? Which would he accept?

I would say in reply that it says in the Bible that when the Babylonian king was having a feast a hand appeared and wrote on the wall "Mene, mene, Tekel, Up-harsin,"-"Counted, counted, weighed and found wanting"-or in today's terms that the Toledo scales showed there was a short weight measure. I think, Mr. Speaker, if we have people to inspect scales to make sure they are giving accurate measure we should also inspect all packages to see that their prepackaged measure is accurate.
I would like to refer again to the committee set up by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. On August 10 the minister announced the appointment of a committee, the consumers advisory committee, and she said, as recorded at page 6581 of Hansard, that it is to do the following:
(a) To consider and advise the minister on such questions relating to the operation of the Food and Drugs Act and the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act as she may refer to the committee; and (b) to give consideration and advice to the minister on such matters relating to the operation of the Food and Drugs Act and the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act from the point of view of consumer interest as the committee shall see fit.
I do believe the very important matter raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North in this bill will be of great concern to that committee, and will certainly give guidance to them in their meetings.
The hon. member referred to Senator Hart of the United States senate and said his bill was inspired by the Hart bill. I would like to read a comment made by Senator Hart before the 47th national conference on weights and measures in 1962, the report of which was published by the United States department of commerce. He said this:
It seems to me that what is required are definite standards against which packages and labels can be measured. Enforcement then requires only measurement against the standard; not a determination of whose definition of "conspicuousness" or "misleading" is correct.
Standards, whether in the law or in regulation, give to the manufacturer greater freedom to compete on the basis of price and quality. He can plan his merchandizing campaign knowing that his competitor will be held to the same packaging and labeling standards as himself. And he can spend the large sums necessary for packaging and labeling equipment, materials and printing, secure in the knowledge that his packages and labels conform to the law and regulations because the law is certain and precise.


The hon. gentleman who has introduced this bill, No. C-47, merits the thanks of the house for having brought the matter up for public discussion. The name of Senator Hart's bill, to which reference has been made, is the truth in packaging bill. In this country the problems raised in the hon. member's bill are of concern to the Department of Trade and Commerce, and also to the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Fisheries, and some of the matters raised in this bill are not related to the Weights and Measures Act which it is seeking to amend. In fact I do not know if some of the matters raised in this bill are within the competence of this parliament because some lawyers think they are trespassing on provincial jurisdiction. Certainly many of the items in it have a great deal of merit. Clause l(p) speaks of weight, measure, quantity or count, and this adds nothing to our existing law except "count." It is doubtful if that type of regulation, that kind of item or that type of consideration will come under the Weights and Measures Act. Certainly under the Criminal Code of Canada miscount is an offence.
With reference to clause l(q)(i) it speaks of "standard size designation," and I am doubtful about this. I am not a lawyer, but I believe legal opinion would not support this because "standard size designation" could come within provincial government jurisdiction.
Clause l(q)(ii) reads:
-the net quantity of the contents of any prepackaged goods, in terms of weight, measure or count, that shall constitute a serving and shall be used where the goods are in a wrapper or container-
It is doubtful if "serving" would come within the competence of the Weights and Measures Act.
Clause 1 (qXiii) reads:
.. .the standard quantative designation of the contents of any prepackaged goods that shall be used when the net quantity of the contents cannot meaningly be designated in terms of weight, measure or count,...
This refers to quality and it seems to me that the acts of this parliament cannot ensure quality of performance to satisfy the anticipations of the customer. It seems to me that is a rather broad conception.
Subclause (qXiv) certainly has merit, as do (rXi) and (rXii). Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to read a quotation from the Cohen report on English company law, where it said this:

No system can wholly protect fools from their own folly or from the knavery of others, and the advantages of trying to do so as fully as possible have to be weighed against the disadvantages of imposing fetters on business conducted honestly and efficiently.
Merchandising is changing so rapidly and the power of advertising in our society is so persuasive that the questions raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orli-kow) have a special meaning. We could well look at our federal legislation, and the provinces could well look at their legislation, to see whether the problems to which the hon. member has drawn attention are being adequately dealt with.

speechtext: I think truth in packaging in the House of Commons would be a good idea, too.

It would be a good idea, but what I want to make clear to my hon. friends opposite is that a bill of this type has, first of all, a technical aspect and requires the advice of experts in the commercial publicity field. As everybody can see, the bill is rather difficult to read and even to understand on account of what I would term the jumble of our legal terms. Is it not contrary to the parliamentary reforms advocated by our hon. friends opposite to consider matters requiring technical knowledge, the hearing of witnesses and which, more or less, call for some kind of survey in order to ascertain to what extent the public is being misled and to what extent also the people are satisfied?
I fail to see how a parliament could lose one hour of its time to consider amending a paragraph or a section, among several, in an act lost in a jumble of other legislation connected with administrative law. As this seems to be nothing but an administrative matter, parliament should not be bothered with it for a whole hour, when there are other very urgent problems to settle. We should not be bothered or importuned with such technical details.
I feel that at certain times, legislators should confine themselves to matters of great scope dealing with major and important principles. They should not be asked to devote

one hour of their time uselessly, since it seems that the bill is not going to be passed.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question? Does he not realize that this bill is so drafted that it would give to the administration the opportunity to make all the regulations? Does he not realize that the bill actually meets the very point he is making; that we should not deal with it here but that we give the power to make regulations to the government?

Mr. Speaker, what the hon. member says is partly true, but should parliament devote its efforts to those little regulations, or rather put all its energy into working out an over-all type of legislation? I think this belongs in the administrative field; each department employs legal advisers who are able to see and find out how the consumers are to be protected. They are aware of any restrictions which should be imposed on dealers and merchants who might take advantage of the consumers in general. This is strictly our administrative matter. The government provides in each department, for legal advisers who are paid with the people's money and who are responsible for advising the government with regard to the form of each piece of legislation, so as to make it more adaptable and useful in its practical application.
That is precisely why I cannot understand that the hon. member who introduced the bill, who calls himself a member of a reform party, should ask the house to waste its time in considering technicalities. Therefore, I think that rather we should ask the legal advisers of the department concerned for their opinion. Indeed, we see that by asking for expert advice-and I am not thinking of legal advisers, because I have had no contact with them-but after consulting knowledgeable people in this field, we have been informed that this bill will alter precisely nothing from a practical point of view. Even if it were passed as it now stands, consumers would have the same protection and dealers would be limited by the same restrictions. Consequently, Mr. Speaker, parliament has been down-graded by a useless logomachy whereas it should have been maintained on a proper plane.
That is why I am disgusted with the hour spent in discussion of insignificant details which merely concern the opinion or legal advice of the department concerned.
